subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: The House resumed from May 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-ll, an Act to provide borrowing authority, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to speak on Bill C-ll, the Bill to borrow $24.8 billion. Since this Government will doubtless spend this money according to the Budget that the Minister has brought in, I cannot agree with burdening our country with further debt at this time. What the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) proposes is a budget for big business. It is not the budget that a great many people in Canada have asked for. It is a budget that was asked for by a very few pressure groups such as the Business Council on National Issues, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. The sort of things that they asked for were to make a big issue of cutting the deficit, and that this should be cut by $7 billion, and that the cuts should be done largely in expenditure and particularly in the social programs of the Government.
They also asked that social programs be "targeted to those in need". In other words, they asked that there be an end to the principle of universality. They have asked that tax hikes only be temporary, and that the manufacturers' tax be replaced with a sales tax. Obviously, they did not ask that that be temporary. These groups asked that there should be a discontinuation or reduction of industrial grants and subsidies for regional development, and that preference be given to keeping the interest rates high until the deficit goes down, rather than vice versa. It was never once suggested that the deficit be
May 16, 1989

reduced by having companies pay the $30 billion or so of deferred taxes which would have wiped out at least one year's deficit.
Generally speaking, this Budget has followed their requests very closely. In the constituency that I represent, Trinity-Spadina, there has been some study of the Budget and questioning of people on the streets to get their opinions. A few of the comments we have received in the course of that inquiry are as follows: A writer tells me that her income has been cut by 10 per cent by order of the Cabinet, in that what was originally for her a $40 fee for the library's use of her book is now only a $36 fee.
There is also a problem with regard to our university in that we could now more easily lose our scientists to the United States because the free trade deal makes it more inviting for post-doctoral students to go to the United States. The student's spouse can more easily find employment there. Naturally, that could be very attractive to those two individuals. It means, however, that we will probably lose potential scientists from Canada. Also, the Government's funding program holds back on direct funding to basic science at the university and ties government funding more and more to the interests of specific private enterprises; that is to say, dollar for dollar matching of grants from industries. Therefore, the study of science is suffering, and that is of great concern to many people in Trinity-Spadina.
There are other concerns. For example, the carving away of something like $800 million from our unemployment insurance benefits. The people of Spadina are not encouraged when they find that after the benefits have been restricted, some of the money that they pay for unemployment insurance will be used for the Government's training programs for which they have very limited respect, if any. In addition to that, they point out that the Government is getting out of its responsibility for keeping the unemployment insurance viable, especially by regional supplements. Almost half a century of undertakings have been broken by the Governments of Canada to the people of Canada to provide a cushion for people who are forced into transition.
My constituents are also concerned that the Government's promise that the social programs will not be cut, promises that were made not very credibly by leaders of business before the election, have not been met. Some business leaders have since clarified their credibility by
Borrowing Authority
reneging on those promises and demanding exactly what we knew they were privately demanding, that the social programs be cut. Therefore, the Government has cut about $175 million this year out of the promised child care program, and it is cutting about $4 billion over the next four years in what would have provided spaces for some of the 200,000 who badly need them. At the same time, the Government is continuing with a $4,000 child care tax deduction which can benefit only the more affluent members of society.
I have a long list. I cannot go through all of it, though I would like to. They are particularly concerned with the attack on universality by renaming it with a newly coined word, the "claw-back". They agree that what is implied there is that the rich in Canada are not taxed now by this Government according to their ability to pay.
The Government has sharply reduced the tax on rich people and, therefore, has raised the tax on middle and low income people. As a supposed substitute for fair taxation, it now wishes to establish the principle of taking back with the right hand what it gives with the left hand. It gives people the old age security pension and then takes it away again, not by taxing them according to their ability to pay, but by taxing them because, as Canadian citizens, they relied on what was understood to be their right, and to which they had been contributing through their work and their taxes. In fact, it will mean that some people who earn over $50,000 who are not pensioners will pay less tax than some people earning over $50,000 who are pensioners. There is no reason or rationale for that distinction.
There have been further cuts to our cultural industries, and that is a very strong concern in the Trinity- Spadina area of Toronto. Many people work in the cultural industries and many people are heavy users of the cultural industries. The CBC has been cut back in four successive years. Now it has been cut back by a further $140 million. After promising up and down that the cultural industries were not on the bargaining table with the United States, the Government does what the competitors in the United States dearly wanted, and it is cutting the $55 million postal subsidy that we have been giving to our publishers and periodicals. Part of the means of keeping Canada together over great distances has been the subsidy to our publishers and periodicals and the Government has decided to wipe that out, no

May 16, 1989
Borrowing Authority
doubt on the principle of harmonizing with the United States.
According to the Budget, we are taxing a working poor family 44 per cent more than the Government found when it came into office four years ago. Tkxes have already gone up for the poorest workers by 44 per cent, for middle income people by 10 per cent, and for upper income families taxes have been reduced by six per cent. It is no wonder that people are complaining about the taxes while the Government puts up a show of being concerned about the deficit. The Government will not tax those who have the money. It will not even force those who owe the tax to pay the tax, if they are wealthy corporations. Yet, if they are individuals, they have to pay interest on unpaid tax, and that has been increased from one per cent to two per cent.
The Government is accelerating a trend which has been in the wrong direction for some years. For example, comparing personal and corporation income tax and sales tax between 1984-85 and 1987-88, personal tax increased by 54 per cent in total. Between 1984-85 and 1987 corporate tax increased only 16 per cent. Sales tax increased by 48 per cent. The taxes paid by low and middle income people, equally with rich people, have increased. The taxes that are the special moral and social responsibility of rich people have not, by any means, kept pace with them.
In Toronto we have a very serious housing problem. It is not the only part of the country with this problem, but there is a serious housing problem in Toronto. It is even hitting the corporations now because their employees quit their jobs and move out of town, or desired employees refuse to come to town because of house prices. For example, in Toronto a detached bungalow costs one-third more than it cost one year ago, according to a report in The Globe and Mail yesterday. There are also significant increases in places such as Kingston, Kitchener, Calgary, North Vancouver, and Victoria.
However, the rate of increase in Toronto is twice the rate of increase in the highest other city. The only immediate manner in which to check that would be to increase the budget for social housing. Instead, the Government has cut $2.3 million out of the funds for co-op and non-profit housing. A more long range way to put a brake on unreasonable house price increases would
be a speculation tax. Obviously that would take longer, being a legislative matter, but it should also be done. However, the Government shows no interest in that either.
Finally, the Government is putting on this big song and dance about cutting the deficit, not loading things on to future generations, and not even looking after children in this generation, but it still maintains the billion dollar give-away that it gave last year in order to win the by-election in Lac-Saint-Jean for a future Tory Cabinet Minister. The Government's claim that it has to cut the deficit is not believed by the people in the riding of Trinity-Spadina, or elsewhere in Canada.
I wish to move on to another matter that also concerns many of the people who live in the riding of Trinity- Spadina and elsewhere. That is the Government's military budget. It is called Defence, but in some ways it is not a Defence budget, it is a war budget. There is a great deal of pleasure in the fact that the nuclear powered submarines have been dropped, at least for this year. There was overwhelming pressure from the Canadian public to do that, and it has also been reported that, for its own reasons, the American Government was not supportive of letting us have the technology for the nuclear powered submarines. However, whatever the reasons, people were glad that it was done. However, they notice that otherwise the Government has made the cuts in the wrong places.
It chose to cut Canadian bases, including the one at Summerside which provides an important search and rescue service. This is important for civilians as well as for the military. However, there has been no cut in the wholly unnecessary $1.2 billion funding for Canadian troops in Europe. Whatever was the rationale 40 years ago has disappeared with changes in western Europe, changes in eastern Europe, and changes in the world as a whole. To continue blowing over $1 billion to keep a token force there in order to keep alive the fears generated 40 years ago is both a waste of money and is burdening our children and grandchildren, as the Minister keeps warning us. It is also a disservice to the cause of peace and the resolution of the arms race.
The Government is also still blowing hundreds of millions of dollars, perhaps not all in one year, but over a period of time, in building up its base at Goose Bay in the
May 16, 1989

hope that we can peddle it to NATO for a NATO training base. It is willing to ignore the protests of the Innu people, as it is willing to ignore the protests of the Quebec people who are affected by the same low-level flight training, because of a greedy notion that, if NATO establishes a base at Goose Bay, there will be big revenues to Canada. It continues with the low level flight training which is damaging the environment and ruining the lives of people who have lived in that area, some of them for generations, up to 8,000 years.
Furthermore, the Government is still subsidizing the export of military goods. Call them arms or weapons or military equipment, they are used by people who use force either against another country or against their own citizens.
The DIPP grants in the range of $250 million will be cut by $25 million per year perhaps starting two years from now if the Government does not change its mind, as it often does.
Some of the companies that receive the subsidies for manufacturing arms will be coming as exhibitors to the Annex fair in a couple of weeks at Landsdowne Park in this city. The Government will send its military representatives to give their blessing to the arms fair and it will give free entry to people from countries like Chile, El Salvador, South Korea, Indonesia, Thrkey and many Middle Eastern countries that have very bad records for using such weapons against their civilian population. There is no interest in justice as a basis for peace in this Government. It is simply a matter of any opportunity for its friends to make a buck.
The same attitude applies to the Third World, the former European colonies, colonies from which European nations over the centuries took untold billions of dollars worth of gold, silver, lumber, agricultural products and forced labour. They are now, in the reckoning of our banks, debtors to us and they are being pressured by Governments, including Canada, putting pressure on little Guyana, for example, to accept so-called austerity measures which means more starvation for those people so the wealthy of Canada can grow still wealthier.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will finish simply by saying that one recommendation being made publicly for a fairer tax system and a fairer Budget is the wealth tax. The Government makes a tiny gesture toward that in its large corporation tax but it excludes many of the people and corporations that ought to be paying under a wealth tax. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with some interest to the remarks of the Hon. Member. I want to make a comment and then ask him a question.
My comment is with respect to national defence. During the 1988 election campaign and for months prior to that, we heard from Members of the New Democratic Party and, unfortunately, in many cases from Members of the Liberal Party that the cure to financing child care and a variety of social programs was to cut back on national defence expenditures. They said this country was spending too much on national defence. In the 1988-89 fiscal year, our nation spent over $11 billion in our national defence effort. That is very close to 10 per cent of the total Budget, if one excludes debt carrying charges, so one gets an idea of what an enormous expense it was. Yet this country was willing to bear that expense because it is in our national interest and the interest of our international sovereignty.
Notwithstanding that, time and time again we were told to cut national defence, cut this program and that program. In the Budget recently passed by this House, we did reduce our national defence increase in expenditures. But what do we hear from the Opposition? We hear howls of protest. They say we should not have cut back on this expenditure or cut back on that program. Every day in the House we hear complaints about the closing of bases like Summerside. What were they

May 16, 1989
Borrowing Authority
talking about when they said to cut back on national defence expenditures? Did they not realize that this would be the result? Did they not realize that service personnel numbers would have to be reduced, that bases would have to be reduced, and programs would have to be reduced?
How many times have we heard a Member of the New Democratic Party and, unfortunately, Members of the Liberal Party say no to nuclear powered submarines? We cancelled that program, but what do we hear? We hear complaints about national defence cut-backs. We just heard them from the Member of the New Democratic Party.
The Hon. Member said if we tax the rich and the corporations, we can solve our financial problems. As a matter of record, personal income as a percentage of gross domestic product has increased fairly dramatically in the past number of years. It now amounts to some 86 per cent of GDP as opposed to 76 per cent a few years ago. There is a reason why there is a new balance between personal incomes and corporate incomes.
If we tax the rich, and take every penny that the so-called rich of Canada make and put them in our tax coffers, and if we tax the large corporations and profit-producing corporations even to the last penny, what will happen? Will the rich not leave the country? We will have no one to tax. Will the corporations not find other means to finance themselves? Do not all Canadian citizens pay all the corporate expenses?
I do not understand how a Member can stand in the House of Commons and suggest that as a solution, unless he tells us what will happen if that action is taken by the Government with respect to the so-called rich of Canada and the so-called rich corporations.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his two questions, one implied and the other explicit.
The implied question was about our attitude to cuts in defence. Yes, we wanted cuts in the defence budget. We wanted cuts particularly in the nuclear powered submarines and we are very glad that public pressure has brought that about. However, we also wanted cuts in the useless and provocative expenditure in Europe. That has
not been touched. Instead, the Government appears to have played a little game.
Years ago I was on city council. If there was talk of cutting the public works budget, the proposal that was always made by the very clever commissioner of public works would be to cut out the men and women who go down the street with a broom and bag to pick up the litter. Of course there would be a public outcry not to cut those jobs.
In other words, the Government has chosen to make the most unpopular cuts that it could, mostly in opposition ridings, as was pointed out, in order to take public attention away from the fact that it is still intends to increase the arms budget by about 5 per cent per year. It has been going up by about 6 per cent per year, much higher than the general rate of government expenditure. It still intends to continue that foolish expenditure in Europe. Our position is not that there should be no defence-none of us has said that. I do not know about the Liberals, however, what we want is a more reasonable approach to the expense. That is what the Government has refused.
As for the matter of whether or not the wealthy people will leave Canada, if we consider the wealth tax that I have suggested we will see that we are almost the only industrial country in the world that does not have a wealth tax. If we tax the wealthy in Canada they cannot run to the United States, Britain, France or Germany to escape a wealth tax.
Furthermore, if we tax them now they will not have time to take all our oil, all our gas, all our lumber, all our minerals, all our fresh water and all our electrical power with them. In other words, if they leave the country they will to that extent begin to lose control over that which gives them wealth. I believe they will do as they do in other countries. That is to say stay here and accept a more reasonable net income rather than the extraordinary incomes the owners of wealth receive in Canada now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make on both the question of my hon. colleague from Halifax West and the presentation of my colleague from Trinity-Spadina.
May 16, 1989

I would like to set the record straight on a number of issues. To begin with, since I have been a Member of this House I do not remember one member of the Liberal Party making any comments about reducing defence, or the moneys to be allocated to defence. As a matter of fact, I believe that we are very cognizant of the spending on defence. I did a quick survey about three and a half years ago and found that the money that was being spent on defence even by the Government across the way was equivalent per capita to what Canadians spend eating in restaurants.
On the second point concerning the nuclear submarines, I want to make a couple of things clear. This Party has always been very much in favour of a strong navy, a three-ocean navy.
In terms of the issue of nuclear submarines, they were sold to us on the basis that their acquisition was to guard our sovereignty. We had French fishermen catching four times what they were allocated in the southern part of Newfoundland and the Government did not seem to do anything about that sovereignty issue. We did not need nuclear submarines to go under the ice to tell us what is happening in southern Newfoundland. If we could not do anything about the sovereignty in the south of Newfoundland, what were we going to do under the ice if we did see a submarine there that was not Canadian? What were we going to do? I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, and you can take it from me that if you do not know in the nuclear submarine business what you are going to do within seconds after detecting another one, you are just as well off not being in the business.
My main concern right now in defence is quite opposite from what the Hon. Member has said with respect to NATO. I am concerned now that we have made some commitments. We have 6,000 troops in Europe. We have a commitment to reinforce them with 5,000 more. We have plans for tanks for $2.4 billion to be delivered in 1992. What has happened to all that? What are the Europeans saying? What will the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) say when he goes over to Europe at the end of May? I would be very interested to know that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to have the opportunity today to comment on the borrowing Bill. This is something that I have been looking forward to with great anticipation as the machinations of this place carry on. It is something that a number of Members have made comments on.
I apologize in advance if perhaps occasionally I appear parochial and talk a little bit too much about Newfoundland and Labrador.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: So long as you are not partisan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I am never partisan-perhaps parochial. However, the interests of my province are something that matter a great deal to me and, if I may point out, something that matters a great deal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government.
This is a Budget that is important to the country and important to everyone in it. It is a Budget that without question takes some very stiff measures, but measures that only react to very stiff times. It is a Budget that we were told in advance would demand sacrifice of all Canadians. However, we were told quite specifically by both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that those Canadians who were least able to bear the burden would be those who would not be asked to bear the burden.
While the Budget may be tough, it is also fair. It is fair primarily for that reason. The people in the country, either geographically or economically, have been asked to make the least of the sacrifices. That is particularly the case in Newfoundland and Labrador.
We have to deal with the growing national debt, the debt that is growing by $3 million an hour, $80 million a day-and $1 billibn every two weeks. It is a debt that is demanding interest that totals $39 billion this year and will consume 35 cents of every dollar we take in to pay the debt and the interest on that debt. That is more than health care, family allowances, Old Age Security and social assistance put together.

May 16, 1989
Borrowing Authority
When Members opposite speak about protecting our social programs, surely there can be no better way than protect the amount of resources that go into those programs from going out in interest and in principal payments on the debt. If we do not address that problem quickly it will get bigger and the pressures will get bigger. If there is nothing more in hand to do to address the needs of social programs and protect those social programs for all Canadians, it is attacking the debt and the burden that the debt puts upon us.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Why didn't you do it before the election?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It took this Government two terms to undo the situation the Liberal Government of 1980-84 put us in, to get us back to where the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), the Minister of Finance in the previous Government, had us. He had us at $13 billion, and by 1993 we will get there. We continue to carry the burden of the hon. crowd opposite. I suspect we will for years to come.
With $6 billion more this year in interest payments, we had to take action. If we are to have an increase of $6 billion, we have to take it from a number of other places. The balance between tax increases and reductions is fair. It addresses the problem. More important, it allows us in the years to come to be able to continue to address our problems, and at the same time to continue to be able to provide the services, to provide the programs that Canadians so long have expected and so long have depended upon.
I would like to comment a little, if I may, on the economic performance of the last few years, the economic performance of the Government in partnership and co-operation with Canadians, provincial Governments, businesses, workers and those who want to create jobs and wealth so that more jobs can be created. Together, it has been successful.
In the last four years we have seen one and a half million new jobs in Canada. It is important for Canadians to know that together with their Government they can create jobs, that together we can move ahead to create new opportunities.
In Newfoundland and Labrador, and again I apologize for being parochial but it is important and this is a good story to tell, we have seen strong economic growth-10,000 new jobs in 1988 alone, in one year, were created. In four years we had a fall in the unemployment
rate of more than 8 per cent-the largest decrease in the unemployment rate for any province in the country over that period of time.
The outlook for the economies are good, with 2 per cent growth through the balance of this year and into next year, and 3 per cent growth after that.
I would like to comment if I could on regional development which is something that I am sure my friend opposite from Burgeo will comment on later this morning or later today.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak today on this borrowing Bill and about the debt and deficits of the country. I believe historians will look back on these debates at this time in Canada's history and see it as a strategic time when the Government of the people had to act decisively. That is exactly what our Government is doing.
I am proud to represent the riding of Markham, which also takes in Whitchurch and Stouffville. It has 160,000 people and includes many small and large businesses. Most important, it has a lot of astute people.
I have been quite impressed with the general comments on the Budget. The only complaints I have received so far are that we did not go far enough in expenditure cuts. That is a topic that I intend to pursue.

May 16, 1989
Borrowing Authority
This Government introduced a massive review of expenditures under the Neilsen task force. Over a thousand programs were reviewed, and hundreds of people with expertise in the private sector reviewed it. I want to ensure that we got every bit of value we could from that excellent and thorough review.
In September, 1984, Canadians gave the Government a mandate to get the economy back on track. In November, 1988, that mandate was reaffirmed. In 1984 we made a thorough study of the nation's economic problems and came to some sobering conclusions. Not only were these problems deep rooted, they had been aggravated over the years by misdirected government efforts to deal with them.
What past Governments really had been trying to deal with were the symptoms of economic weakness, not the causes. We decided it was time to get back to basics, time to get to the source of the country's difficulties. We introduced a comprehensive agenda for economic renewal in the fall of 1984. This agenda was designed to rebuild the foundations and provide a strong framework of economic growth. It was meant to provide a better climate of confidence.
One step was to change FIRA, the investment agency. Not only did we change the name to Investment Canada, we changed its mandate to welcome investment in this country.
Another step was the privatization of a number of Crown Corporations. If it does not serve a public policy role, it should not be run by Government.
De Havilland was privatized and we know the success story of that company. Forty-five per cent of Air Canada is in private hands now and I understand that the other 55 per cent will be moved shortly.
A number of these steps gave investors and Canadian business men and women more confidence in this country. There has been an explosion of jobs since we began those efforts in 1984, with over 1.5 million jobs. The unemployment rate dropped sharply.
Between 1984 and 1988, jobs were created at a faster rate in Canada than any other major OECD nation. The report shows that the Canadian economy grew faster in 1988 than any of the seven OECD nations, except Japan, with real economic growth last year of 4.3 per cent. This
surpassed the OECD June 1988 projection of only 4 per cent.
The OECD projects that Canada's economic growth will slow to 3.1 per cent this year, following behind that of Japan and Italy, and to 2.9 per cent in 1990, second only to Japan. The report also shows that Canada led the G-7 nations in employment growth in 1988, and will continue to do so both this year and in 1990, with the unemployment rate falling again.
These results are proof positive that the agenda of the Conservative Government is working and that Canadians are responding to the opportunities presented by our actions. That does not mean that we should rest on our laurels. Canadians must make their way in an increasingly competitive world economy. To succeed in world markets we must continue the progress we have made in implementing our agenda. One of the keys to success is deficit reduction.
We cannot pass on to our children and grandchildren a crippling legacy of debt. We have already made great strides toward fiscal responsibility, but we cannot rest.
When we came to office the deficit was more than $38 billion, as my colleague mentioned in a question a few minutes ago. The national debt had doubled in just three years. The private sector was being stifled by regulation and wasteful Government intervention in its affairs.
We acted quickly. Since we took office the deficit has been cut by almost one-quarter in dollar terms and almost in half in relation to the economy. However, there is still much to be done.
Canada's current deficit of $30 billion is quite simply the difference between what the Government spends and what it collects in revenue. For every $3 the Government spends it borrows $1 at this time. That is how serious the situation is.
Just to dwell on the background a little, in the second half of the 1970s real growth dropped sharply while the rate of inflation was high. Combined with the income tax indexation in 1974, and the indexation of major transfers to provinces, these factors generally took a significant drop in revenue growth at a time when expenditures were rising rapidly. Weak economic growth led to a number of measures to promote growth in employment during the second half of the 1970s, including the federal tax reduction, the exemption for interest and
May 16, 1989

dividend income and selective sales tax exemptions. These measures intensified the deficit problem.
In the early 1980s real interest rates rose sharply and the economy was hit by a severe recession. Expenditures aimed at mitigating the effects of the recession rose rapidly. Revenue growth dropped sharply because of the weakness of the economy. Interest rates rose to record levels as the deficit widened, leading to unprecedented increases in debt service charges. These developments led to a rapid increase in the public debt which now stands at $325 billion.
The national debt has and will continue to increase rapidly. By the end of the Trudeau era the debt had reached over $200 billion. Since then it has continued to grow, largely due to the interest charges it has accumulated.
You may be interested to know, Mr. Speaker, if you go back to 1958, which is not so long ago, that our entire expenditures as a Government amounted to $5.8 billion. The current Budget is $142 billion. The size of Government has to be attacked, and that is being done by this Government.
To see when the last surplus was, we have to go back to 1969-70 when there was a surplus of $332 million. At the end of the next five years ending in 1974-75 we saw the deficit rise to a mere $2 billion. In the next five years which ended in 1979-80 the deficit had risen five times to over $11 billion. In the next five-year period under the Liberals it grew to over an astonishing $38 billion. That is when we took over as a Government, when we started to steer the country in the proper healthy direction.

CANADIAN DAIRY INDUSTRY-PROTEST CAPPING OF MILK PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian dairy industry is facing a very serious crisis. While the Government claims that it is defending our producer controlled marketing systems, which are totally permissible under the General Agreement on Thrifts and Trade, the Government has decided to cap industrial milk prices until December, 1990 to implement decreases in industrial milk prices, and if the cost of production formula goes down, to ask the provinces to extend the cap on prices of fluid milk.
These decisions have been made as a result of the April, 1989 GATT negotiations and are contrary to the clear advice given by the dairy farmers of Canada. To add insult to injury, the Wilson Budget is reducing dairy programs by $14 million.
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, our marketing systems here in Canada are permissible under Article 11 of GATT, yet this Government has completely ignored that status. In fact, it is like shutting the door after the cows have left the bam.
The decision to cap milk prices makes no sense under the circumstances. Milk prices respond to changes in cost of production. Production is controlled through the quota system with the producer carrying the cost of surplus disposal, if any. Canadian producers and the Canadian market are not distorting export markets.

NATIONAL CAMPAIGN FOR ACTION ON TOBACCO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada must "treat the tobacco epidemic like an epidemic". This is the theme of the

National Campaign for Action on Tobacco which begins today.
Last year, more than 35,000 Canadians died from diseases caused by tobacco. This total is greater than the total number of people who died as a result of accidents, suicides, homicides, AIDS, alcohol and alcohol-related fatalities all combined.
Indeed, the Government has acknowledged that cigarette smoking is a national health problem of substantial and pressing concern and one that is of epidemic proportions.
Thus, it is a sad commentary that the Non-Smokers' Health Act, which was passed by Parliament in June, 1988, with support from all three political Parties, has still not been proclaimed by this Government almost a year later.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that now would be a fitting time for the Government of Canada to take action: to proclaim this Act and make it law and thereby allow the will of Parliament to prevail.

TRIBUTE TO CANADIAN NURSES AND ORDERLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer some words of encouragement to male and female nurses in Beauce, Quebec, and throughout Canada who are a credit to the nursing profession and work very hard to alleviate the pain and suffering of hospital patients. I pay tribute to them because they go beyond what they are professionally trained to do: they bring compassion to nursing care.
It takes more than just knowledge to do this work, Mr. Speaker. It takes tireless dedication and respect for every human being. It used to be called a vocation, and even in our modem society, there is still room for nurses who give their patients sympathy and hope. In addition to their work, there is always a high degree of personal dedication.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that health care authorities will give these guardians of the health of the people of Beauce, the people of Quebec and the people of Canada the consideration they deserve. On the other hand,
members of the nursing profession would be better off if they stayed on the job and relied on public opinion, which is behind them all the way.

subtopic: RELOCATION OF ANTIGONISH OFFICE

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
subtopic: RELOCATION OF ANTIGONISH OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Health and Welfare Canada currently maintains a district office for income security programs in Antigonish, Nova Scotia. This office processes claims for Canada pension plan benefits, family allowance and old age security payments from local offices in Amherst, Truro, and New Glasgow. In addition, it receives claims directly from the counties of Antigonish and Guysborough.
This office has been providing efficient service to the public since 1966. The public facilities there are ideally suited to this purpose. The staff is competent and dedicated. However, I have recently learned that plans are afoot to move the district office to New Glasgow. I suggest that this would be a serious mistake. Service to our seniors would be disrupted and in all likelihood new office facilities will have to be constructed. I cannot see how this could be justified either from a program delivery or cost-effectiveness viewpoint.
I urge this Government to have regard for the service to our growing seniors population in eastern Nova Scotia and not to proceed with this move.

subtopic: BENEFITS RECOGNIZED
BENEFITS RECOGNIZED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with great interest that I have noted a change in the song Premier Peterson is singing about the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. We have all known Mr. Peterson as a great opponent of the trade agreement before it was signed. Recently, however, Mr. Peterson was in France extolling the virtues of the trade agreement. He is now encouraging the French business community to take advantage of the agreement and the decision by the European community to form a single market in 1992 by expanding and liberalizing trade between Europe and North America.

May 16, 1989
Our federal Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) is being echoed by the Ontario Trade Minister who has told French investors that the agreement provides them with an excellent opportunity to enter the U.S. market through Canada.
It is good to know that opponents of the Free Trade Agreement are finally recognizing the benefits it provides.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXEMPTIONS FOR HANDICAPPED
REQUEST FOR EXEMPTIONS FOR HANDICAPPED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada's copyright legislation has for many years protected the handicapped. In the past, an approach to the creators was made and accommodation was granted.
Bill C-60 amended the Copyright Act in 1988 to bring it into line with today's world of television, photocopiers and satellites. The handicapped have consistently requested that a new exception be put in the copyright law for the production of the special format materials such as Braille and talking books. Such an exemption would eliminate existing requirements to obtain the copyright owner's permission.
Until these amendments are introduced, Mr. Speaker, the visually handicapped and the institutions which serve them, including the CNIB, the MAB and the Institute Nazareth Louise Braille could be faced with charges which would gravely compromise their operations. Our Government must act to perpetuate essential services to the visually handicapped.

subtopic: PROTEST AGAINST PENSION CLAW-BACK PROVISION
PROTEST AGAINST PENSION CLAW-BACK PROVISION
speechtext:

I would like to place on the record the names of a number of seniors' organizations who have written or telegraphed their disapproval of the attack on pensions. They are: One Voice. National Pensioners and Senior Citizens Federation, Action Now, Canadian Council of Retirees, Nova Scotia Federation of Senior Citizens, Cape Breton Council of Senior Citizens and Pensioners, United Senior Citizens of Ontario, Golden Age Club of Montreal, Federal Superannuates, Association of Jewish Seniors, Ontario Seniors Coalition, and SOAR, the Steelworkers Organization of Active Retirees. The Minister must name those seniors' groups who support the Government's pension measures or apologize to all seniors in their organizations for putting words in their words and speaking on their behalf.

subtopic: REPLACEMENT OF SALMON RIVER BRIDGE NEAR TRURO
REPLACEMENT OF SALMON RIVER BRIDGE NEAR TRURO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Salmon River bridge near Truro, Nova Scotia is a CN overhead bridge crossing six sets of railway tracks and is in a drastic state of deterioration. The capacity rating of this CN bridge has been repeatedly reduced to
May 16, 1989

the point where it cannot legally accommodate anything more than a half ton truck.
The National Transportation Agency, CN, the Department of Highways, consulting engineers, and anyone with common sense, agree that this must be replaced immediately. The tracks in question divide the community of Salmon River right down the middle and are a barrier for school buses, ambulances, firefighting equipment. The bridge is absolutely essential as a main thoroughfare.
On January 27 of this year the NTA issued an order to CN to provide plans for a new bridge within 90 days. That time has now come and gone. With all due respect, I call on the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) to apply his influence and to expedite the process to replace this hazardous CN bridge which affects the lives of everybody in Salmon River.

Atlantic Canada that is far in excess of any that was available before from any government in Ottawa.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister who is obviously responsible for newspeak in this Government, the Minister who is responsible for telling us that reprofiling means something other than cuts, how he can justify standing up in this House and still trying to persuade Canadians that what he is doing is something other than a savage attack on Atlantic Canada and the people in Atlantic Canada?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1989 may well go down in history as the year the fishery died in Canada. In February, the Minister of Fisheries, who I am glad to see back in his seat-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what do you say to thousands of fishermen and plant workers whose livelihoods are being wiped out by this Government's mismanagement and its lack of policy on foreign overfishing? speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
subtopic: OVER-FISHING BY FOREIGN VESSELS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:

Mr. Speaker, the Government is asking Members today to adopt Bill C-ll, giving it the authority to borrow $24.8 billion. Members on this side of the House obviously cannot support this legislation, and let me tell you why.
Since the tabling of the Budget last month, constituents in Kenora-Rainy River have been flooding my office with telephone calls, asking me how this Government can be so insensitive and inconsiderate.

My constituents also believe that this Government could have reduced spending. Instead, the Government is asking to borrow billions and billions of dollars.
I never thought it possible for a government to tax dreams but obviously I was wrong. This Government has broken so many promises, it is no wonder that Canadians have become skeptical of the political process. This Government has put an end to Canada's unique social programs. The Minister could have used his influence and prevented the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) from making promises he could
not keep. He would not be asking Members to approve a borrowing authority of some $24.8 billion.
The threat to Canada's social programs is real. This Government promised to maintain the sacred trust of universality. Instead, the Minister of Finance has once again decided that senior citizens are second-class citizens. This Government is taking advantage of the vulnerability of seniors by taxing back old age security pensions. Canadians preparing for their retirement years are now doing so with the knowledge that their future may not be as secure as they had thought.
There are many single parent families in Canada today, Mr. Speaker, earning $50,000 a year and supporting one, two or three children on this salary. ment rate of 7.3 per cent is clouded. The 1986 census figures show an unemployment rate of 9.9 per cent. It is Canada's young people who will be severely affected by the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
When the Government talks about securing the future for the next generation, it should look at what it is doing to future generations with these measures.
This Government cannot be trusted to pursue deficit reduction in a manner which is fair and equitable to all Canadians. Low and middle-income families have seen their taxes rise faster than taxes on upper-income families. Taxes paid by the traditional family, with one income and two children, earning only a poverty line income, has seen their taxes increase by 61 per cent, compared to 8 per cent for a family making $100,000. Where is the fairness in the tax system?
This Budget is nothing but a Tory tax grab. Once again large corporations walk away without having to pay taxes and Canadian citizens cany the burden. When you combine all the tax increases announced in this Budget, individuals are paying six times greater than corporations. Tax increases totalling some $2.6 billion for individuals, versus tax increases for corporations of $410 million, are not what I call a fair distribution of the burden, nor do I call this tax reform.
The excise tax measures announced in this Budget, and more particularly, the two-cent a litre increase in gasoline prices will contribute further to an already depressed region in my riding.
People from northwestern Ontario pay astronomical prices for gasoline. In Pickle Lake, for example, one litre of unleaded gasoline is sold for 61.9 cents. Residents of northwestern Ontario are fed up with this Government's taxation policies. They want a tax system which is fair and equitable. They are prepared to share the burden, but they are not prepared to carry the burden alone. My constituents have told me that deficit reduction was of primary importance to them. But they also told me that government spending was out of control and that they wanted to see measures which

would narrow the gap between the rich and the poor. I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that my constituents have been thoroughly disappointed.
This Government also said it was committed to regional development. The Prime Minister first demonstrated this Government's commitment to regional development when he failed to appoint a Cabinet Minister from northern Ontario. People from northern Ontario are not represented at the cabinet table and do not believe this Government is committed to regional development. VIA Rail needs to replace its antiquated equipment with modem equipment. This will allow it to remain competitive. It must be allowed to keep its fares at competitive rates. There is no doubt in my mind that the CBC will have no other alternative but to reduce services, Canadian programming, and it will be forced to close stations across the country and lay off a significant number of people.
Once again, Canadians in rural areas will be the recipients of these cut-backs. Once again, this Government has broken its promise. Crop Insurance Program. The federal Government is once again attempting to shift the burden to the provinces.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise again in the House and take part in the debate on Bill C-ll, known under its short title as the Borrowing Authority Act, 1989-90.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to get a clear picture of the present budgetary situation if we are to understand what the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will do. Canadians have a serious problem: a large and growing public debt. An hour from now, that debt will have grown by $3 million. In just two weeks, it will have grown by more than $1 billion. The interest payments on the debt are also increasing rapidly. Only 20 years ago, just 12 cents of every dollar taxpayers sent to Ottawa went to interest payments. When the Progressive Conservative Government came to power in September 1984, that figure had already increased to 32 cents. This year, 35 cents of every tax dollar will be used to service the debt. The recent surge of interest rates shows how much our huge debt has left us exposed. In just one year, the projected cost of paying the interest on the debt has risen by more than $6 billion. This year alone, interest will cost us $39 billion, and a sudden rise in interest rates would have a devastating effect.
Mr. Speaker, how did we acquire this enormous debt? Quite simply, Canada did it by living beyond its means. The debt put us in an untenable position, and the present Government is determined to take the necessary measures. This Budget acknowledges the fact that maintaining social programs and the standard of living that Canadians want for themselves and for their children
Borrowing Authority
requires a vigorous debt reduction program. The Progressive Conservative Government has already made considerable progress in this respect. We have succeeded in reducing the growth of the debt from almost 24 per cent in 1984 to less than 10 per cent last year. Despite that progress, the debt is continuing to grow more rapidly than our national income. That is why, considering the urgency of the situation, the Minister of Finance has embarked on this series of budgetary restrictions. We shall proceed with reductions in Government spending affecting a wide range of programs.
Mr. Speaker, the Budget also proposes revenue increases affecting corporate and personal income taxes, sales taxation and the financing of the unemployment insurance program. These debt control actions will amount to more than $5 billion this year and $9 billion next year. The Budget measures will cut the annual deficit in half to $15 billion by 1993-94. Financial requirements, in other words, the money the Government must borrow, will be down from $20 billion this year to $3 billion. As the deficit goes down, the debt will shrink as a proportion of our national income.
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to reduce the deficit, but the Budget ensures that the total package of measures is balanced, reflecting regional circumstances and placing the greater burden on those who are better able to cany it.
That is why this Budget talks about building for the future, not borrowing from it. That is why this Budget deals vigorously with the main obstacles that separate us from that future, the problems of a growing debt. Successful debt control seems to entail a very high cost, but it is nothing compared to the price we will have to pay if we fail. One of the measures in this Budget, Mr. Speaker, which clearly reflects the balance and fairness of this Budget and this Government, concerns repayment of family allowance and old age security benefits by high-income taxpayers. The Government is spending $30 million more in 1988-89 on direct income support for Canadians than on any other program, and we cannot make significant fiscal progress without examining this area of spending as well.
Canadians 65 and older are entitled to the old age security pension and families with dependent children under 18 are entitled to family allowance payments.

May 16, 1989
Borrowing Authority
Regardless of the assistance they really need, these payments are subject to individual income tax.
Mr. Speaker, this Budget proposes to claw-back these payments from high-income Canadians. They will refund old age security and family allowance benefits at the rate of 15 per cent of individual net income over $50,000. The repayments will be calculated on the income tax return and will be deductible in computing the balance of tax payable.
The $50,000 cut-off means that only high-income Canadians will have to repay benefits. Low- and middle-income taxpayers will not be affected.
This measure will be phased in over three years. In 1989, actual repayments will only be one third of the amounts repayable. In 1990, they will be two thirds. Full repayments will only be required starting in 1991.
Once the system is in place, 54,000 old age pension recipients with high incomes will repay all their benefits and 74,000 will repay part. Overall, Mr. Speaker, only 4.3 per cent of all old age pensioners will be affected, with 1.8 per cent repaying all their old age security pensions.
As for family allowances, it is expected that 368,000 high-income families will repay all the allowances received and that 167,000 will repay part. In all, 14 per cent of family allowance recipients will be affected.
This measure is in keeping with the universality of these transfer programs. All eligible individuals will continue to receive benefits, regardless of their income. Those most in need of assistance, Mr. Speaker, will continue to keep all their benefits. Thus social security nets are maintained, while helping to ensure a solid financial basis for social programs in the future.
Mr. Speaker, very recently in this House, we saw the ardent defender of widows and orphans, the Hon. Member for Laurier-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), rise to defend the rich and thus abandon those whom he has long claimed to defend.
Mr. Speaker, we saw the same reactions from Liberal and New Democratic Members, these Robin Hoods get up in the House and protect and defend those whom they usually consider to be rich. Such hypocrites, Mr. Speaker! And Canadians have been witnesses to this hypocrisy, Mr. Speaker.
And what about the most recent attempt, which I could not overlook today, by the Liberal Senate, once again, to override the will of the people democratically expressed last November 21, by acting again in a way that is unacceptable to the people, Mr. Speaker. This really shows us the rage and frustration of those who not so long ago were responsible for Canada's present financial situation, who believe that power is theirs by divine right and use the pretext of tradition to trample underfoot the democratic will of a whole people.
This also shows us, Mr. Speaker, the need to do some house-cleaning there. When we hear Senator Gigantes say, as he did this morning on the radio: "We want to teach the Government a lesson, to show it that it is misbehaving."
Mr. Speaker, it is not misbehaving to serve the people and to shoulder one's responsibilities as a government and we certainly have no lesson to learn from those people. It is a hostage-taking and again, the hostages are the Canadian people.
It is never pleasant for anyone, any Canadian, to have money taken from them in order to pay off debts. It is not fun for me either and we should certainly not expect people to shout and jump for joy over this situation. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, I am banking on the maturity of Canadians and of my constituents who understand the situation very well, who know the causes very well and who are satisfied with the performance of the Government and its Finance Minister who, instead of taking one-shot measures and hiding the truth as our predecessors did, is proposing solutions that will protect and guarantee the future of all of us and will help reach that high level of excellence of which we are capable.
Excellence, Mr. Speaker, does not just happen. It is the reward of hard labour. Only great strength of character makes it possible to persevere, to make efforts whose effects are not perceived, like the movement of the hand of a watch, tireless but imperceptible.
Reaching a high level of excellence is difficult and maintaining it is even harder, for the search for excellence implies continual striving to do better.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the real tradition to which Canadians are attached, values of excellence, values of democracy and the desire for a better, prosperous future.
May 16, 1989

This Budget will give back to this country the freedom of action needed to maintain social programs and our quality of life.

It introduces the brave new world of free trade in which ordinary Canadians will pay $1,700 more in taxes while big business calls the shots. Members opposite know that my constituency of Prince Albert used to be represented by the late John Diefenbaker. There is a clear feeling that the Conservative Party, which western Canadians nurtured through its years as opposition, has turned its back on western Canada now that it is the Government.
May 16, 1989

My criticism of the Budget is simply that I believe it is bone-headed economics. All Canadians recognize that there is a debt problem and that we cannot indefinitely spend money that we do not take in. We all want to be able to afford future programs.
However, I believe the way to solve this type of problem is to create opportunities for people who do not have those opportunities and are not contributing taxes to the nation. The Government should create opportunities for people who are unable to develop businesses or create jobs so they may have the futures they would like.
There are many people in my constituency who would like to contribute more, but the Government has taken away that opportunity.
For instance, the people in the co-operative sector can contribute much to this country. Forty-three per cent of Canadians belong to a co-op, and 70,000 people work for co-ops. The financial co-ops have $60 billion in assets, while retail co-ops have $16 billion in sales. It is a major sector of the economy that could play a key role, particularly in the post-free trade era, in ensuring that development was sustained in the communities and regions affected by the Free Trade Agreement.
The co-op sector was looking for some help in regard to dividends. Presently, there is a serious disincentive for people to invest in co-ops compared to other forms of business.
The housing co-op sector feels strongly that it was sold out when its commitment of 5,000 housing units was cut to 1,800. The co-operative sector was disappointed that the Government took no action when Ministers responsible for co-operatives identified health and worker co-ops as ways to save money and jobs in this country.
Official development assistance was drastically cut, yet the co-op sector has played a key role in providing international assistance and developing links between Canadians and people in other countries. They helped to ensure that Canada would play its role in the world community. We cannot continue to prosper as a nation if we turn our neighbours throughout the world into beggars.
The community development sector would also like to contribute. One would think a Conservative Govem-

ment that supposedly believes in self-reliance and initiative would want to encourage groups that help people pull themselves up by their own bootstraps. Instead, the Government cut Secretary of State programs which allowed those groups to organize.

During the election campaign the major issue was honesty and integrity in Government. As I went door to door, clearly, that was the question that was raised most frequently. Frankly, I can tell Hon. Members, and I say this with a great deal of sincerity, the Canadian public is starting to lose faith in political Parties and politicians generally.
They have also spoken to me about the Throne Speech. They feel, and they are not necessarily members of my Party, that there were a lot of old ideas that were rehashed, and that there were repeated statements and announcements to make the Government look good.
For example, we heard before the election about the Centre for Sustainable Development. We heard it mentioned again in the Throne Speech. We look in the Budget and yet we can find no trace of it. We have not heard recently either of the National Centre for Disease Control that was promised for Manitoba, or the research into aging, or the Diagnostic Research Centre at St. Boniface Hospital. We are wondering what has happened to all of those great statements because frankly, there were many Manitobans who had hoped that they might come through.
What is the Budget all about? Canadians, not only in my constituency but people with whom I have talked across the country, have described it as the most massive tax grab that we have ever had in this country. It is a Budget of broken promises and misleading statements. Where is the vision in the Throne Speech or in the Budget? Where can Canadians, the poor, the middle class, the older worker, the seniors, the students, the women and the single parents go for solace? Where do they go for hope, for comfort, for reassurance that things will be better in the future. Clearly, ladies and gentlemen, not to this Government.
It is a Budget of broken promises and misleading information. This Government has practised that with a great deal of skill. Let me share some of these with you that are on the public record. The Government talks about the deficit being over $38 billion in 1984. It forgets to remind Canadians, however, that it was in power for more than half the year. If it had not been, its line would be, of course, "It would be greater than what it was." The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) was saying during the election and prior to that that the deficit was under control. Well, he forgot to say that they had doubled the
May 16, 1989

debt. It will have doubled in over five years. The deficit is higher today than it was during last year, and it is about the same as it was the year before.
Conservative Members like to brag about the 1.5 million jobs that have been created. However, they do not want to tell us where those jobs are and what proportion are part-time jobs. This is the Government that tried to deindex the pensions for the aged. It was unsuccessful because the seniors stood up to it. I am proud that the seniors were able to do that. Now the Government comes in with a more clever scheme. It is called clawback. What are people saying about that? Well, initially if one examines it, one feels somewhat sympathetic to people having more money returned. However, if we look into it further, if we realize that if we were to change that figure one little bit, the ravages of inflation of one year will cut that roughly by half.
We also realize that the Government can change that figure at any time, and of course Canadians believe that that figure will change. They remember the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) saying that unemployment would not be touched. This is what I mean by a misleading statement. Well, it was not touched, it was mangled. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has received a lot of good comments from his colleagues, and I appreciate that they think so highly of him, but this same Minister-some people call him "Honest Mike"-did say during the election that all of that which was being promised were not promises, they were election commitments. They were within the fiscal framework of the
Borrowing Authority
Government. Well, let me ask the Minister and his colleagues to tell that to the women regarding child care. Tell that to Canadian people. Ask them whether or not those were in fact commitments rather than promises. You know, Mr. Speaker, it was the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) who said that VIA Rail would be improved, that all would be rosy for VIA Rail. What has happened? It is another misleading statement. It was another statement that was not carried through. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said that Air Canada was not for sale. Well, they sold one-half of it and they are about to sell the other half.
The Prime Minister said that they would increase foreign aid and it has been reduced. Many Ministers said that there would be no cuts in regional development. If you believe that you were not at Question Period today, and you have not been listening to what has been happening in western Canada.
This Government said that it would be a fair government. We just heard that comment a moment ago from the Member opposite. Ask the people from Summerside if it is a fair government. Ask the people from Portage la Prairie if it is a fair government. Ask the people from any number of communities across Canada how fair it has been.
What has it done to the commitment to housing? Nothing. What has it done to the CBC? Reductions, gutting it. What has it done to the Post Office? Reduced the service. It brought in privatization and deregulation en masse that are going to cause us all kinds of difficulties.
Look at the area of health and education. There are reductions in transfer payments, reductions in training and retraining, reductions or freezes in student aid. It has made no significant advances in the area of education. I cannot imagine how one could possibly be a Member of this Government and brag. I would not dare brag. I would be too humiliated to do so.
The people of Canada are starting to react to this Budget. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, there will be some significant reaction as they get to know more clearly the massive impact that this Budget will have on Canadians. They will be standing up. Some of us think that this flood of information that they have received has been deliberate and it has been confusing people because there has been so much of it. We have been using large numbers with which they are not terribly familiar. Once they get

through all of that, you mark my words, there are going to be reactions that you have never dreamt possible.
The Government has the gall to call its advertising program education. We all know it is not education. Let us call it what it is. It is propaganda.
It is propaganda to try to make us feel guilty about the standard of living that we have accumulated in this country, to try to make us feel guilty about all of the social programs that we have. Government Members have not told us that there are a number of countries in this world that are spending more of their wealth toward social programs. They are trying to pit us against each other in order to come out the winners.
There has been a massive and unfair tax grab. The top 1 per cent are now gaining $3,570, the bottom 10 per cent, $90. The average disposable income is down by 1.4 per cent since 1984. Some people paid tax increases of over 60 per cent. They pretend that education is the cornerstone of competitive society and they have slashed programs in those areas. They have slashed them in a very savage kind of way.

Mr. Speaker, if we look, for instance at education and especially at transfer payments, we see that in 1985, there was a cutback of over $8 billion in the areas of health and education. Another more recent cutback will probably get us down to $4 billion. In training and skills upgrading, we see that over $200 million, originally earmarked for community colleges, has been redirected. On research and development, despite recent increases, the Government is spending only half the amount spent by the United States, Sweden and Japan. Student assistance funding has been frozen, and the criteria have not changed since 1984. In the area of literacy programs, for instance, the Government announced a subsidy of $110 million but didn't say this will be spread over four or five years, and will cover five million Canadians.
That is just a few dollars for every person in need of this training. There is talk of capping post-secondary education grants for Native people. Classes for new Canadians have been abolished and with them the
language training they were receiving. There were also reductions and cutbacks in the multiculturalism program and funding for groups representing women, official language minorities and again, our Native people. And there are some very important items in education.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I want to say that the honesty and integrity of this Government are being questioned. There is a growing sense of cynicism across Canada and, I say this in all sincerity, what the Government has done is shift money around. Cutbacks will put the tax burden on Canadians in the provinces and the territories, and we will see that individuals will have to pay more, a lot more!

I must say that through its own incompetence in managing the affairs of this country over the last four years, the Government is indeed mortgaging the future of our youth, perhaps to a degree that will cause the young men and women of Canada not only to lose their exuberance for life but perhaps even their faith in this country.
Young people have dreams, and how cruel it would be to take them all away in one fell swoop. What would this one fell swoop be? It is commonly known as the dastardly Budget. This is exactly what the Government is doing when it cuts back on funds to education, training and research. These cuts lead directly to missed opportunities and, for these young people, to a loss of the fulfilment of their dreams. There is so much promise in our youth. Why is it that they cannot have the same hopes that we had when we were growing up? But, no, this Government chooses to cut back, to take away the tools that they will need for the fulfilment of their hopes.
May 16, 1989

Are you aware that after accidents suicide is the second highest cause of death among today's teens, Mr. Speaker? This is a chilling indictment for Canada and I would suggest for the present Government. Education is more than a right. It is an investment.
This Government wants to talk about free trade. I have a feeling that the Minister, who is pushing free trade and the almighty dollar, is looking at this investment in education as only an expenditure. Education must be in line with other aspects of free trade because our young people must compete sooner or later with their American and Japanese counterparts in business.
In my home town of Welland a science fair was organized recently, and this was what The Welland Tribune had to say about it on April 3, 1989:
Environment issues appear to be important to many of today's elementary and secondary school students. It shows in the entries at this year's Niagara Regional Science and Engineering Fair, now being held at Niagara College. Be it recycling, acid rain, the greenhouse effect, cleaning up of oil spills-
I could refer to the one we have just experienced on the West Coast. It continued:
-or keeping our air and water clean, there is a research project or experiment about it.
The interest is so great in this fair that the community has had to impose a maximum participation of 300 entries for the simple reason that there is no more space to display other experiments.
I mentioned that the Government is mortgaging the future of our youth. The least it could do is to give our young the tools with which to work. That is education. By cutting back the Government is taking away the tools of our children.
In spite of this accounting sleight of hand in the Budget, it is obvious that post-secondary funding has decreased under the terms of the present Budget. In fact, we are looking at a decrease here in Ontario of $70 million to $75 million in the year 1990-91 and about $200 million across the country. If this is not taking the money out of the hands of our youth, I do not know what is. I suggest that this Government is seriously short changing our most precious asset, our youth, our leaders of tomorrow.
I see two Members in the House who, like me, are from the Niagara Peninsula. I am sure the House is aware that 75 per cent of the tender fruit of Canada is
Borrowing Authority
produced in the Niagara Peninsula. Why am I mentioning this now? It is because I want to underline something which has taken place in the very recent past having to do with the Chilean grapes being taken off stands. Two grapes in a shipment of 200,000 cases showed the presence of three-tenths of a milligram of cyanide. The Government immediately took not only Chilean grapes off the shelves but also all vegetables from Chile. What does that have to do with us? This is no more or no less than agricultural terrorism.
Can we imagine what would happen if some deviant dumped some cyanide into a grain car? Our prairie farmers would be devastated. What would happen if someone found a tainted British Columbia apple at Christmas time? Would all the apples be taken off the market? God forbid. What would happen in the Niagara Peninsula if this year someone were to find cyanide in some of our magnificent peaches, cherries, raspberries or strawberries? Would the whole crop be cancelled if only two were found to be tainted? I suggest the drastic over-reaction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Beatty) left Canada vulnerable to all sorts of bizarre scenarios and to agricultural terrorism.
Canada's image as a trustworthy trading partner has suffered severely. Some countries are already requesting cash for their produce when our credit was acceptable before.
The impact on consumers when the Chilean grapes were taken off the market was immediate. Consumers paid $4 to $6 per pound for grapes while Chilean grapes could have been sold for $2 a pound. I wonder who pocketed all that extra money. For fruit importers the effects were also immediately devastating and will affect them for a long time to come.
We learned of one importer who had a weekly payroll of $70,000. Some 40 per cent of his business was in Chilean grapes. He sent urgent pleas for help to the Government which went unheeded and unanswered. Importers asked the Government for inspection so that they would not have to throw away perfectly good fruit. In one case the produce from one company had a value of $1 million. A simple inspection could have averted extreme measures and unnecessary loss of money and food. The industry even offered to pay for the inspections, but all urgent appeals to save businesses were not acknowledged.

May 16, 1989
Borrowing Authority
I have researched this matter, Mr. Speaker. On April 4, Mr. Art Fisher of Fisher Brothers in Montreal, sent a letter to a Dr. Liston, Health and Welfare, which read:
-the detention orders which were issued only for the older fruits by Agriculture Canada's inspectors state that all fruits are now suspected of violation. Would you be kind enough to advise what tests and efforts, if any, were made by Agriculture Canada or Health and Welfare to confirm these suspicions. Are new fruits the subject of the same suspicion? If so, on what basis?
I would like to know which statutory law governs the alleged violations. Is it a violation of a particular regulation or not? If so, which one?
Aren't these legitimate questions, Mr. Speaker? The writer went on to say:
I feel that I have the right to know under which authority and on what basis you claim to have the right to seize our produce.
I believe that we in this House have the right to know on what basis the Government made this particular decision.
Mr. Fisher and all other fruit importers and producers rightly feel cheated, abandoned and ignored by the Government. Americans sold the same produce and seem to be making money. It should be noted that there was not even one incident of ill effects reported from the consumption of the produce.
I appeal to the House and to Ministers involved not to react so quickly in these cases. Sooner or later we in Canada will be drastically affected by this agricultural terrorism.
