Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the borrowing Bill which is of concern to all Canadians. The people of my riding are deeply concerned about this Bill. Small businesses, seniors, and agricultural producers all have great concerns.
Interest rates are at an all time high. This is not good for small businesses. It may be good for the people of Toronto and it may help to keep the economy of Toronto down, but it is certainly not doing any good for the City of Moose Jaw and the businesses there. Saskatchewan has the highest percentage of small businesses of any place in Canada. Small business people are drastically hurt by high interest rates.
Small business has been hurt by the recent cuts of $2.6 billion in the unemployment insurance scheme. This has put pressure on not only workers but on small businesses. The unemployment insurance scheme is to be funded solely by the workers and the employers. That will mean that premiums will increase. It is unfortunate that unemployment insurance will have to be funded on the backs of small businesses.
The federal sales tax which will be introduced in the near future will be very disruptive for small businesses. Certainly the tax will remove billions of dollars of purchasing power from consumers. The federal sales tax is a regressive tax in that it hits middle income earners much harder than it will hit higher income earners. When it hits middle income earners, they spend less. Middle income earners spend a larger percentage of their dollars on consumer goods than higher income earners. This will hurt the small businesses of my community as well as those right across Canada.
The Canada Pension Plan has been attacked by the Government's claw back. The pensions of those earning more than $50,000 will be affected. The unfortunate aspect of that is that it is the beginning of the end of universality. The figure is $50,000 this year, but it could easily be moved down. Even if it remains at $50,000, as inflation increases over the years it will affect more and more pensioners. No one on this side of the House disagrees that higher income earners should pay proper and fair taxes, but the tax should be on high incomes rather than on pensions.
The federal sales tax will also hurt seniors. As I said, it is a regressive tax which will eat into the fixed incomes of pensioners. Canadian pensioners live on fixed incomes and many have a difficult time, as it is, managing to get by. A 9 per cent and later on a 10 per cent or 11 per cent federal sales tax will adversely affect them.
Pensioners should not be surprised that the Government did not take them into account when it was drafting the Budget. As Hon. Members will recall this is the same Government which in 1985 wanted to deindex old age pensions. The only reason it backed away from that was that pensioners rose up in great numbers and vehemently opposed that move. In this case, the Government has taken a more tactical route and is removing universality through the back door. This is the same Government that did not consider seniors when it passed the drug patent Act in the last Parliament, an Act which
May 16, 1989

unfortunately for seniors will mean higher drug prices. That is most unfortunate not only for seniors, but all Canadians.
The agricultural sector is of great importance to the Moose Jaw-Lake Centre riding. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) indicated in his budget remarks that the situation in agriculture is improving. The Minister, however, has obviously not visited western Canada lately. He certainly has not been to Saskatchewan where last week it seemed as if half the province was blowing away. There are still severe problems in agriculture in western Canada, and the agricultural sector is still going through a very difficult phase.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) suggested that producers buy crop insurance. That is all very well, but in the Budget, we note that crop insurance will be cut by $90 million this year and $110 million next year. This will force the provinces, if they wish to continue the program, to increase the funding of the program drastically.
The Government is in the process of dismantling the entire infrastructure of western Canada. In Saskatchewan, Alberta, and Manitoba, there is in existence an infrastructure that supports the many small communities and family farms that depend on that infrastructure. A life-style has developed since 1905 when the three provinces were incorporated and the Province of Manitoba was expanded. That life-style has developed an infrastructure, and that is now being dismantled.
The branch line rehabilitation program has been cut. This will cause severe hardships for communities as the movement of grain will become much more difficult and expensive. As well, advance payments have been cut. In the past, farmers could get interest-free loans on their grain. Now they will have to borrow money at present interest rates, making it much more expensive for producers.
Before the election the Government was telling a different stoiy. It announced that there would be a drought payment of $850 million to Canadian producers. That promise was made in a last ditch effort to try to save seats in western Canada. Now, according to the Budget, the Government has come up with only $425 million, half of what was originally promised. This is another example of commitments the Government made which
Borrowing Authority
turned out to be nothing more than election profiteering.
I have spoken briefly on things that affect seniors, agricultural producers, and small business. The Budget affects all Canadians. It is an unfortunate fact that the average family is now paying $710 a year more as a result of the Budget. Once the federal sales tax is introduced, it will be paying $1,700 per year more. This is a very unfortunate Budget for the people of my riding and for the people of Canada.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-ll, respecting the borrowing authority. This Bill is reflective and indicative of the Government's mismanagement of monetary and fiscal policy.
If we look at the Government's high interest policy and borrowing practices in the 1988 fiscal year, $5 billion was added to the deficit at interest rates two to three points above the U.S. rate. This self-inflicted pain by the Government is now being transferred to Canadian taxpayers. It now wants Canadians to pay for their mistakes. I hope this Government will lower interest rates this year and thereby reduce the borrowing cost and in turn the budget deficit without inflicting such unbelievable pain on the middle and lower income groups.
Just over two weeks ago the House heard the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) deliver an eloquent speech on the Main Estimates and indirectly the Budget. The Minister gave us his vision for Canada, and I will concede that it was a lovely vision indeed: a competitive nation, a caring, compassionate society, a stronger country with healthy viable regions. I was nearly swept off my feet in the moment myself. I spent the rest of that afternoon trying to find the embodiment of these goals in the Budget. Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that they are not there. When the Budget axe fell, they were its first victims.
I would like to address each one of these goals and point out the Government's failure to deliver at every step of the way. First the Government called for a competitive nation. This country must be competitive if it is to survive the Free Hade Agreement. If this country is to become competitive, it needs to show a real commitment to research and development. The National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, a Board set up by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself, said

Borrowing Authority
that $500 million at a minimum was needed to ensure our future competitiveness. However, the Conservatives have not even set aside half that much.
We are not headed toward self-sufficiency in research and development. We are going in the opposite direction. In fact the numbers show that we have had the lowest commitment to R and D in the G-7 nations.
Where are those worker adjustment programs that were promised? Where are the training and retraining programs that were also promised? Where is the assistance for small business that was promised? So much for our international competitiveness.
Before the Government took office we used to have a caring and compassionate society. Today, care and compassion have become hollow words. Government members pay lip-service to them, but I do not think that they really believe what they are saying. After all, last week we saw Canada's social programs bludgeoned. Universal social programs are now a thing of the past. The Government no longer contributes to UIC, and the programs that remain are increasingly funded on the backs of the people who can least afford to pay. The Tory Government has ended the universality of care and compassion, too.
All this is supposed to lead to a stronger Canada with healthy viable regions. Somewhere there has been a lapse in logic.
The first few months of this Government's mandate has seen the biggest sell-out of regional development programs that this country has ever experienced. Years from now I believe that the Budget will be seen as the measure that ended the viability of our regions once and for all. This may be a vision to the Conservative Government, but to the rest of the country it is a bloody nightmare.
Government members would have us believe that Canadians are dancing in the streets because of the Budget. The reverse is true. Canadians and Londoners specifically genuinely want to help their country in the debt and deficit crises. They also want the Government to put its financial house in order first. Let us not forget that the best of times it has taxed, taxed and taxed in the
past five years, yet it still managed to double the debt. Figure that out. Canadians have.
Second, Canadians want the burden to be shared fairly, especially by higher income groups and large corporations, not on the backs of the middle class. I applaud the efforts of small business, labour, consumers, women's groups, seniors, and others who are now saying that enough is enough.
I would like to turn my attention to the way the Budget will affect my home Town of London. Looking at it from the point of view of the average London family with a moderate income and a couple of children, the Budget is the largest tax grab in Canadian history. Never before have we asked individuals to pay so much more in taxes than we did in previous year.
Naturally we have the tendency to look at the Budget in terms of one year at a time. Let us look back to when the present Conservative Government first came into office. When we do this, we find that the Budget is just one in a long series of massive tax grabs. When we take all of these together, we see that the picture painted by the current Budget of the Finance Minister becomes even uglier. Tbday, after five consecutive Budgets, the average London family earning $32,000 in 1984 has been clobbered by extra taxes amounting to $680 a year and over $2,000 over that five-budget period. In other words, most Londoners today are having to contribute nine more days of wages to the tax man than when the Ibries first came to office.
If only the tax grab were going to stop there, if only the Government would be content with nine more days of a family's wages. Unfortunately Canadians are not so lucky. The fact of the matter is that the Finance Minister has only just begun to pick our pockets. At the beginning of 1991 we are all going to be hit by a goods and services tax, a 9 per cent tax placed on everything we buy and on every service we use. The Government protests that the tax will be revenue neutral.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What a joke.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1989-90 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Yes, it is a joke. We have found out that in fact it is going to be a government money machine that will produce some $10 billion more. In personal terms that represents another $400 a year for every single person, man, women or child or $1,600 for a family of four. The Government has said that some of this money
May 16, 1989

will be returned to Canadians through the tax system, but even with this, the bottom line is that the goods and services tax means money out of their pockets.
In the Budget, London has also been hit very hard by the savage cut to the federal transfer commitments to the provinces. These payments are used to help pay for hospitals and post-secondary institutions. London just happens to be one of the most important centres in the Province of Ontario for both of these. London is one of the province's major medical centres. We have several of the finest hospitals and medical research centres in the world. The loss of funding means first that cuts to services are going to have to be made, throwing trained medical professionals out of work, closing top notch facilities and forcing even more of our top workers to move to the United States. Also over time the quality of health care that Londoners deserve will deteriorate, perhaps at the cost of innocent lives.
As for post-secondary education, I would like to point out that the University of Western Ontario is one of the best in the country. However, the school is already functioning with less money than it needs, and further cuts will seriously affect its academic health. A good university takes decades to build, but only a few years to destroy. The damage done by the Government to the University of Western Ontario will affect this generation and probably the next few ones to follow.
Thus far I have been building a case to prove that the Budget of the Finance Minister is wrong-headed and hurtful to the City of London and the people who live there. However, I have been saving the toughest for last. This cut above everything else makes the Budget totally unacceptable to Londoners, that is, the closing of CFB London. It is nearly impossible to zero in on any one reason the base should be kept open, but CFB London has been at the heart and soul of the City of London for more than a century. The links between the Royal Canadian Regiment and the City of London are strong and deep. Many of my constituents have an emotional attachment both to the regiment and to the Wolsley Barracks buildings. It will take more than a leaked Budget to convince us that they no longer have a place in our city.
The Environment
The loss of the armed forces base will change London economically, too. There are various estimates about what the base contributes to the economy, but it seems that it is at least $65 million a year. That is a big blow to the economy of any town, no matter what size it is. The closure of the base represents a substantial loss of jobs to the city.
CFB London employs about 1,100 people, just over 700 military personnel and about 400 civilians. Each of these people is presented with a difficult choice. They can either move to Petawawa where the Royal Canadian Regiment is slated to go, or they can become unemployed. Either way, it is a traumatic experience and a tragic one when one knows what it can take to be avoided. Yet, it is clear from the documentation supplied by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. McKnight) that the annual savings to the Canadian Government in wages, operations and maintenance will be virtually non-existent.
In closing I say that Canadians are prepared to contribute toward deficit reduction and the debt, but it must be done fairly and equitably. We can build a strong country, a compassionate country, if in fact we start believing in people, investing in people and investing in our institutions so that we can become more competitive in the world tomorrow.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should provide criminal sanctions against corporate officers who knowingly allow their companies to violate Government environmental regulations or otherwise endanger the health and safety of Canadians.

May 16, 1989
The Environment
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure most Members of the House, and certainly most Canadians, would like to see M-100 become an item for consideration by the Government of Canada, and that the appropriate new sections of the Criminal Code be drafted and soon passed by the House.
First, I wish to quote from the April 27, 1987 Department of Justice Criminal Law Review. The Law Reform Commission of Canada published Working Paper No. 44 entitled "Crimes against the Environment" in November, 1985. In that working paper the Commission recommended that Canada's Criminal Code should be amended to create a new offence which would make it a crime to cause or create a risk of death or serious bodily harm by acts and omissions which seriously violate environmental protection laws. It also recommended that there should be a crime of causing or risking an environmental catastrophe even in cases where there are no accompanying harmful human health effects.
There have been many recent issues. There have been, for example, poisoned fuel, the Valdez matter, other oil spills, problems with toxic and hazardous wastes, or atmospheric problems. There are many problems that require this type of addition to the Criminal Code.
As recently as May 11, 1989, The Gazette ran an article entitled: "Most Canadians favour tough action on spills". In that article is states:
Stiff fines, criminal charges against senior oil company executives, tougher regulations and a cleanup fund created by a special tax on shipped oil are among measures finding strong public support-
Nine of 10 respondents saw the Valdez accident as a sign that the government should take a closer look at oil transportation and consider introducing tougher regulations. Fewer than one in 10 were happy with current regulations-
Almost nine of 10 Canadians-94 per cent of Quebecers-favour stiff fines for companies that spill oil while shipping. 84 per cent support criminal charges against senior oil company executives if their company is found to be wilfully negligent in observing safety regulations.
Regarding existing Criminal Code sections the Justice Law Review states:
A number of Provinces suggested that a new crime would be unnecessary if existing sections on criminal negligence, nuisance and mischief were more imaginatively used or amended to enable more effective enforcement.
The only gaps noted were: (a) endangerment of human health and
safety, (b) transporter pollution, and (c) protection of the
environment per se.
Recently, our task force in British Columbia heard from Dr. Murray Rankin of the University of Victoria Law School. He had undertaken an evaluation of waste management permits in British Columbia and found that a staggering three-quarters of waste management permits in areas of the province had been in significant non-compliance for more than one year.
We now know that not only industry is involved in not complying with existing pollution control regulations, but the Government often does not do anything about it.
There has been a series of recent amendments around the world dealing with the serious criminal nature of this matter. In Austria, the Penal Code was amended in 1975 adding sections to punish for wilful or negligent pollution. Portugal's penal code creates a crime for public community dangers and general dangers to human life and health or valuable property. Japan's penal code creates a crime for polluting or adding poisonous material to drinking water or water supply systems. In the United States, states such as New Jersey, New York, and Pennsylvania, following the Model Penal Code have as crimes reckless endangering and crimes causing or risking catastrophes.
We very much need similar types of action here in Canada.
I now wish to quote from a Study Paper in the Administrative Law Series of the Law Reform Commission of Canada. At page 29 it states:
Increasingly, legislation is being amended to provide courts with more innovative sentencing options than simply fines or imprisonment, including powers to suspend licenses in default of payment of any fine owed, to order remedial and preventive action and compensation for pollution victims, to require offenders to publicize their offences and pay for the investigative expenses of agencies.
It is time that we started moving in that direction. Rather than having the environment take all the damage and then forcing taxpayers to pay, it is time that we took the type of innovative Criminal Code sanctions that I am suggesting in relation to those who knowingly and wantonly destroy the environment and put public health at risk.
May 16, 1989

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In the same Study Paper under the heading: "Characterization of the Pollution Offence" it states:
In Canada, prior to the 1970s, courts and legislatures tended to classify offences into essentially two categories: absolute liability and criminal. With absolute liability offences, only proof that the violating act took place is necessary, and a conviction will ensue. The intentions of the accused are not relevant, regardless of whether the offending act was maliciously planned, recklessly negligent, or morally innocent. At the other end of the spectrum, mens rea-a "guilty mind"-must be proven before a conviction for a criminal offence is secured.
At least in relation to the recent criminal conspiracy in relation to poison fuel, I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that you would agree that mens rea could be found.
Under that same heading, it further states:
Characterization of pollution offences as either criminal or absolute liability often determines whether or not an accused will be convicted. If a court concludes that a pollution offence is criminal, so that mens rea must be proven, it can be very difficult to secure convictions, since many acts of pollution are not deliberate (for example, spills) and are perpetrated by corporations (in which case establishing intent for a corporate body can be an extremely onerous task). On the other hand, court characterization of a pollution offence as one of absolute liability means that polluters can be convicted even though they had done everything possible to avoid the discharge.
Prior to the Supreme Court of Canada decision in SaultSte. Marie, in 1978, courts in Canada were reaching inconsistent conclusions- some finding mens rea to be a necessary element, some finding it unnecessary, some providing defences, some not providing defences.
That is why I am suggesting the most broadly based sanctions under the Criminal Code that I quoted earlier.
Under the heading: "Pro-development Tendencies of Government", which is something we must look at very carefully, it states:
For all the media attention it receives, environmental protection often has a relatively low priority in government. This can partly be explained by the fact that, unlike other regulated activities, pollution is usually the by-product of an activity otherwise encouraged by government and society. The extraction and refining of raw materials, the manufacturing of new chemicals and commercial products are activities which are intended to improve our quality of life, and are generally welcomed as such. In addition to the benefits to society, such activities bring many rewards to government by way of personal and corporate tax revenues and the political benefits which flow to governments taking credit for economic prosperity and full employment.
The Environment
In Canada, government and industry often have an extremely close relationship, wedded by common objectives, common attitudes and more concrete ties such as government loans, grants and subsidies. Governments are hungry for revenue and employment-generating projects. In this broader context of government-industry partnerships, environmental protection may not receive the priority it should. Departments of environment are usually considered a junior portfolio within Cabinet, in terms of prestige and power-
Bureaucrats may choose to invoke or not invoke a legal instrument provided him or her for reasons which do not reflect problems with legislation, courts, or his or her political masters.
Bureaucrats may resist initiating formal sanctions because this may mean relinquishing control over a polluter to "the lawyers", an admission of failure of bureaucratic negotiatory techniques. Bureaucrats, many of whom are engineers or scientists, may feel uncomfortable or unfamiliar when dealing with legal jargon, and may prefer to keep communications at a technical level. Some may fear that formal legal sanctions will put bureaucratic practices as much on trial as those of the polluter, and may attract unwanted media attention-Some bureaucrats may be reluctant to adopt an adversarial role with regulatees they have been dealing with a non-confrontational basis for an extended period.
There you have the second major point, Mr. Speaker, and that is that the bureaucracy often fails to live up to the intention of Parliament, or of the Minister, in terms of legislation passed by this House or other Chambers, as well as the problems that they create by not actually laying charges and proceeding with them to the courts as they should. I now want to quote from the report "Improved Program Delivery, Environmental Qualities Strategic Review". It is a follow-on report of the Task Force on Program Review, February 21, 1986. This is the follow-on from the famed Nielsen task force reports. I quote from page 12 where we find the third problem in relation to not having the kind of criminal sanction I suggest:
A thorough comparative analysis be made of the environmental practices followed by Canada and the United States to assess whether they are harmonious both in their design and implementation and that any major discrepancies be taken into account in the ongoing negotiations on free trade between the two countries; new Canadian environmental measures be so designed as to minimize the possibility of countervailing actions.
We now know where the Government is heading. It is hoping to minimize and harmonize, by taking us to the lowest common denominator of environmental control rather than the best.

May 16, 1989
The Environment
Let me continue to quote from the report because even those who were studying it knew what the problems would be:
The regulatory approach is the dominant approach in the United States, and, to a lesser degree in Canada.
There are a number of serious difficulties with the regulatory approach. The first is that the sanctions are often imposed primarily through court actions, and action against each breach of regulations must be the subject of a new court action. Given the difficulty and length of time to implement each action through the court system, the sanctions or fines levied can result in very minimal penalties. Even if legal costs are included, the total cost to the polluter can represent a modest pollution fee. The longer each charge can be prolonged in the court system, the less frequently the fee must be paid, so that the regulatory approach frequently winds up as a battle between lawyers to delay and minimize the payment of pollution charges. In addition, the cost of such actions to the regulator is high.
Once again it is the taxpayer who carries the can and the environment which carries the damage. Certainly that is not an approach to sustainable development for which the Government can continue to pat itself on the back.
A little history is in order. I quote from page 110 of the report:
When the Fathers of Confederation drafted the Constitution Act of 1867, they did not allocate legislative authority on environmental matters to either the federal Parliament or to the Legislatures of the provinces. Without clear responsibility for, or guidance in, the matter of environmental concerns, both levels of Government have, over the years, been able to claim authority for managing environmental problems by taking the position that various aspects of the subject matter fall within their respective areas of competence.
It is generally accepted that the federal argument in favour of its role in environmental protection relies primarily on the "Peace, Order and Good Government" clause of S.91 of the 1867 Constitution Act. Other sources of power, which have been cited to claim the validity of federal environmental legislation, include the regulation of trade 91(2), taxation 91(3), navigation and shipping 91(10), fisheries 91(12) the criminal law 91(27) and the regulation of works or undertakings that are interprovincial or international in nature 92(10)(a) or ones that are declared to be for the general advantage of Canada 92(10)(c). These powers have generally been used in relation to the national interest, international imperatives, health, well being and prosperity of the people of Canada.
I suggest that all of those powers stand behind the argument that I am making here today for amendments to the Criminal Code.
I continue:
Environmental legislation in Canada dates as far back as 1873 with the Navigable Water Protection Act.
The Minister of the Environment has a general responsibility for the resources held in common, such as air (Clean Air Act) and water (Canada Water Act) and for several multi-sectoral issues affecting the environment (Ocean Dumping Control Act, Environmental Contaminants Act).
First, the overlaps and resulting confusion. It should be pointed out that, regarding environmental protection of water alone, eleven major items of legislation can be listed:
the Fisheries Act, the Canada Water Act, the Navigable Waters Act, the International River Improvements Act, the International Boundary Waters Treaty Act, the Northern Inland Waters Act, the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act, the Ocean Dumping Control Act, the Canada Shipping Act, the Canada Oil and Gas Act, and the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act.
Of course we can add to that the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. I quote:
This abundance of legislation has produced confusion as to the occasions on which it is appropriate to use each statute.
The second set of difficulties which should be addressed is with compliance. This can either be encouraged through a variety of means such as formal incentives (licensing, permits, tax expenditures, subsidies, grants, publicity on corporate behaviour) or enforced through disincentives (persuasion, action on licences, Ministerial Orders, civil suits or criminal prosecutions). Federal regulators, in applying some legislation such as the Fisheries Act, generally tend to revert to an ex post facto approach based on disincentives rather than taking the less adversarial, yet more difficult, approach of incentives.
Others, who rely more on voluntary compliance, such as Environment, do not appear to have made full me of the plethora of incentive means available. Part of the reason was attributed to inadequate administrative provisions in the acts they administer.
That is a problem we have created:
Clearly, civil and criminal court actions ought to be considered as
remedies of last resort, when every other effort has failed to produce
appropriate environmental behaviour.
We have reached that stage. There are many corporations that simply do not live up to the regulations passed by Parliament, by provincial legislators or by municipalities. Therefore we must have a broadly-based criminal sanction that can put those kinds of polluters and wilfully negligent individuals behind bars, in some cases for life where they so fully deserve to be. I return to the report:
The allocation of environmental statutes among different responsibility sectors, however, unfortunately gives rise to an ill-structured and uncoordinated federal approach to compliance. For instance, lesser environmental offenders under one federal statute sometimes sustain stiffer penalties than those imposed on other
May 16, 1989

offenders under another statute, for a more serious environmental offence of a similar nature.
Worse yet, some environmental offenders under one given statute, such as Section 33 of the Fisheries Act, often receive a disproportionately low penalty in one region, as compared to that imposed for a very similar offence in another region.
As was said before, the Study Team had access to little information on the extent to which federal regulations, other than S. 33 of the Fisheries Act, are monitored and acted upon. It nevertheless looked at one particular sector of interest: the pulp and paper industry. In the early 1970s, this sector was identified as a major source of pollution and became the first industrial sector subjected to comprehensive effluent standards promulgated, in 1971, under S.33 of the Fisheries Act.
Little action was taken until 1979, when the federal and provincial governments joined forces through the General Development Agreement 1974-1984. The sub-agreements on the Pulp and Paper Modernization Program, implemented through DREE, involved some $544 million of federal/provincial funding ($276 million federal) over a five-year period and were designed to assist in the modernizing of the pulp and paper industry for international competitiveness in keeping with the pre-determined pollution abatement objectives.
Recent media reports and public documents published by DOE suggest that, as a whole, compliance by this industrial sector with the negotiated standards is uneven and lower than had been anticipated in relation to the magnitude of the capital infusion.
Compliance for two of the stated measurement parameters appears to be only 60 per cent and 70 per cent, and for a third (toxicity) it is only approximately 40 per cent.
That simply is not good enough. That is abuse of public trust and of public money.
I conclude with this quote:
The use of criminal sanctions is the fourth area of difficulty which could be addressed. Most federal environmental statutes contain sections of a criminal nature. The Clean Air Act, for instance, prescribes a fine of not more than $200,000 for each offence relating to any emission into the ambient air in contravention of a standard set pursuant to that Act.
The Environmental Contaminants Act sets out a fine of not more than $ 100,000 or a term of imprisonment of not more than one year for any wilful release of a substance specified in the schedule to the Act into the environment, in a quantity or concentration that exceeds the prescribed maximum. The Canada Water Act indicates that a fine of not more than $5,000 per day may be imposed for either the deposit of waste of any type in waters comprising a water quality management area, or for the manufacture or importation into Canada of a cleaning agent that contains a prescribed nutrient in a concentration greater than the prescribed maximum. As pointed out earlier in this report, these statutes have given rise to
The Environment
very few prosecutions: to under the Clean Air Act and none under
each of the Water and Environmental Contaminants Acts.
Those Acts are not working to protect our environment:
In addition to those offences established by the various environmental laws, there exist in the Criminal Code certain offences which could in principle be used to "denounce, condemn and penalize" actions which result in harm to the environment. The most important ones among these are criminal negligence, common nuisance, mischief, causing disturbance, offensive volatile substance, explosive substances and offences against animals. However, as reported by the Law Reform Commission of Canada, "criminal Code offences are seldom used as the basis of prosecutions for conduct seriously harmful or endangering to the environment. Even more seldom are such prosecutions successful".
The Commission attributes this weakness to the narrow and limited arrangement and formulation of the Code in protecting the environment.
At present, the Code contains various offences against persons and other offences against property. The Law Reform Commission's proposal is to add to these a new category of offences against the environment. The principal element of this category of offences would be a single, conceptually unified "crime against the environment". Its role and justification would be to repudiate and deter conduct which seriously compromised the fundamental societal value and right to a safe environment.
The new offence could be formulated broadly enough so that it would be made applicable to a wide range of activities and especially so as not to distinguish between harm to the air, water, land or any combination of these. It could apply to "conduct which seriously damages or endangers the environment by means of direct physical acts or in the course of the manufacture, transportation, use, storage or disposal of any hazardous or potentially hazardous goods, wastes or other contaminants."
The Study Team has not delved into the legal ramifications of the LRC proposal but finds it conceptually compatible with the "cradle to grave" approach espoused by the Minister of the Environment-
I hope all Members will support it, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) for his motion and for the creative, imaginative and vibrant approach that he always brings to matters that are environmental.
His proposal to include crimes against the environment in the Criminal Code definitely appears attractive. Yet the better way is to work on improving and enforcing civil law and, in particular, to improve enforcing and broadening the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. For example, it would be a good step to make clear in the

May 16, 1989
The Environment
Environmental Protection Act the fact that corporate executives are personally accountable for the pollution of their corporations. This personal accountability has to be established.
The Hon. Member made reference in the last few minutes of his extremely fast overview to the Law Reform Commission report. It is necessary to do that because in the same breath the Law Reform Commission pointed out that the Criminal Code perse cannot protect the environment for its own sake, but only if there is a threat to property, to a person or to human life in general.
On the other hand, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act could protect the environment for its own sake. I am sure that that is what the Hon. member for Skeena has in mind as a major thrust of his motion. Therefore criminal action alone has a very narrow application.
In addition to that we have to keep an eye on the enforcement, application and compliance of existing laws, an aspect which is of immense importance. Yet here, Mr. Speaker, I must draw to your attention that unfortunately today in Canada we have weak enforcement at the federal level. We have weak compliance. Why? Because of the lack of funds resulting from budgetary cuts in November, 1984, and in subsequent years by the present Government. It is because of the fact that Environment Canada was for years denied in its budgets the ability at least to keep up with inflation. In essence it is because the Government does not practice what it preaches when it comes to the crunch.
The second point that must be made in this debate is that when in committee a year ago we debated the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the Government refused to move on some very important elements which would have helped enormously to achieve the major goal and thrust of the motion by the Hon. Member for Skeena today. For instance, because of the ideology that is embedded in the Meech Lake Accord the then Minister of the Environment had to come to committee to ask for a change in his own Bill to abandon the power to issue enforceable national standards. Imagine that, Mr. Speaker. That occurred in committee on the initiative of the Minister himself who came and asked to dilute and water down his own Bill. The debate was hot and heavy on that occasion. When the matter came to report stage in this House the Speaker even allowed an
amendment which had been defeated in committee, which would rule it out in principle because of the significance of this issue, namely, the setting of national standards.
When it came to the question of PCBs all the provinces had been exempted from federal PCB storage programs except for Prince Edward Island, as reported in The Globe and Mail just a few days ago. This scenario was predicted by the proponents, those of us who insisted on national standards. However, the Government claimed it would never happen. We knew at that time that no province can impose, for instance, a fine of $1 million as envisaged under the Environmental Protection Act. At this stage the federal Minister can only enforce his law in one province and the territories when it comes to PCB storage standards.
It is important also to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that because of the opposition of the Government a citizen cannot seek an injunction under the Environmental Protection Act, something which we urged the Government to do when we debated the Bill. Under the Act as it is written now the Minister of the Environment is the only person in Canada who can seek an injunction to stop pollution.
Because of the negativism of the Government when we were in committee we could not make the release of any toxic substance a violation by inserting a clause in that Bill called a general prohibition clause. This would have allowed the Minister to stop any pollution and not just the release of the nine substances listed in the schedules of the Act.
The Government said no to removing the requirement that makes mandatory in the drafting of regulations, consultation with the provinces. The new PCB standards are the evidence of the inability of the present federal Government to provide a strong federal presence in the environment.
Finally, the Government again said no last year to the idea that would have made the Minister of the Environment responsible for the monitoring and enforcement of environmental performance by other federal Departments and by federal agencies. As the Act was finally written by sheer majority force-and brutish force I would say-the Minister of the Environment must get the concurrence today under the Act. He must get the blessing, the permission of the Minister responsible for the pollution created by another federal Department or
May 16, 1989

agency before regulations can be made or before the Canadian Environmental Act can be enforced.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this motion. I support the suggestion by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) that anyone who contaminates the environment should be penalized. This suggestion is compatible with the "polluter-pay" principle. It is an excellent deterrent. In this way, we would give economic value to our natural resources which support life itself: the air we breathe, the water we drink and the ground that produces our food.
The Hon. Member's suggestion, although a good one, is nevertheless unoriginal. In June 1988, the Government acquired the tools it needed to prosecute polluters by proclaiming the Environmental Protection Act. This law is intended to protect the health and environment of Canadians through the management of toxic substances that pollute the environment.

The Canadian Environmental Protection Act addresses pollution problems on land, in animal and plant life, in lakes, rivers and oceans, and in the air. It provides the legislative basis for controlling international environmental degradation through restrictions on the import and export of toxic and hazardous substances and through the regulation of Canadian sources of transboundary air pollution.
The Environment
The Act deals with organic and inorganic substances, the products of biotechnology, emissions, effluents and wastes. The Act also establishes a comprehensive scheme for management of toxic substances. However, it is in the area of enforcement where we find coincidence with the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton)
Enforcement is a vital aspect of the legislation. A program of inspections complemented by spot checks is being put in place to verify compliance with the new Act and its regulations. The frequency of inspections will be determined by the risk that a substance or activity presents to the environment or to human health, and the compliance record of the given individual, company or government Department or agency.
Violators can be subject to warnings, orders, tickets, prosecution, and recovery of costs. The particular response will depend on the nature of the violation, the effectiveness of achieving compliance with the Act within the shortest possible time frame, and the likelihood of no further occurrence of the violation. The Act includes significant penalties, ranging from fines of $200,000 a day and six months in jail, to fines of $1 million a day and three to five years in jail. For offences involving criminal negligence life imprisonment is possible.
Jail sentences are an importance enforcement tool under CEPA. There are, however, a number of other effective sanctions specified in the law. We have heard some talk from the opposition Members about sanctions. I think it is important for them to hear what some of them are: seizure and detention, forfeiture, prosecution under the Criminal Code for serious offences resulting in death or bodily harm to another person, court orders, publication by the Minister of the facts relating to an offence, additional fines to negate the financial benefits of an offence, compensation for loss of or damage to property, ticketing, court injunctions on the application of the Minister, civil suits and injunctions on the application of those damaged by the polluter.
I believe that an example is in order with respect to these options and the actions one can foresee by following them. As spelled out, for example, in the court orders in Section 130 of the Act, not only might an individual or a corporation be found guilty of violating a regulatory requirement, they might also be obliged by the courts to keep the peace and be of good behaviour, report to and be under the supervision of a probation officer, remedy or prevent any harm to the environment,

May 16, 1989
The Environment
publish the facts relating to a conviction, notify an aggrieved party of the facts of a prosecution, post a bond to ensure compliance with court order, submit information with respect to subsequent activities, pay the cost of any remedial preventive actions, perform community service, and pay for research into the ecological use and disposal of the substance in respect of which an offence was committed. The thesis behind the enforcement provisions of CEPA is quite clearly to encourage compliance through strong disincentives.
Under Section 122 of the legislation, directors and officers can be held personally liable for offences committed by their corporations. The statement was made on the other side of the House that the whole law was too lax and that there were no actions to be taken against gross polluters. Clearly there is an action in a court order against corporations. While this Government is not planning to undertake witch-hunts or to make scapegoats of individual employees, we will take a tough stand on polluters. The CEPA specifies in Section 115 that those persons or corporations who knowingly disregard regulations will be prosecuted under the Criminal Code. It is these sections in CEPA that makes the Member's motion redundant.
I would like to clarify that our objective is to protect the environment. We plan to pursue that objective. The prosecution of corporate officers or other individuals within a company is but one of the approaches available to us under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part today in the debate on environmental protection. I cannot but praise the interest shown by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) and the initiative he has taken, but I have some

doubts as to the effectiveness of the approach he has suggested.
Environmental issues are very important to Canadians. Our Government shares that view and has made environmental protection one of its priorities, both nationally and internationally. We are aware of the real cost of the deterioration of the environment, and we have established a powerful battery of legislation to fight pollution, one example being the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
To manage the environment, we have taken the offensive on two fronts. First, we mainly try to anticipate and prevent environmental damage before it occurs. We have also built a legal foundation that will help us reach that objective. Second, the Government is aware of the need to deal with pollution problems that have their origins in the past. Together with various companies and with provincial and municipal governments, we have embarked on a number of projects designed to provide solutions to the problems in their present form. I shall, if I may, expand on each of those approaches.
First, anticipation and prevention. On June 30, 1988, after a year's consideration in the House, the Canadian Environmental Protection Act was ratified. Its objective is to prevent all forms of toxic contamination that are a threat to human and environmental health. The legislation enables us to deal with questions as complex as air and water pollution, management of toxic substances, elimination of waste, acid rain and the warming of our climate. The Canadian Environmental Protection Act is based on previous environmental protection legislation including the former Environmental Contaminants Act and the Clean Air Act.
Invoking the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, our Government has established a number of national regulatory standards aimed at eliminating or reducing the threat to our environment. We have also adopted regulations providing for a 50 per cent reduction in ozone-depleting substances, and we also plan to introduce additional control measures that will virtually eliminate such substances.
We are demanding that lead additives be virtually eliminated from the manufacture of gasoline as of December 1,1990. We have issued national standards for the storage of PCBs. We are anxious to take steps in
The Environment
connection with Canada's contribution to the acid rain problem and have established standards for the reduction of sulphur dioxide emissions. Enforcement of these standards currently comes under provincial jurisdiction but could be covered by regulations adopted under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act.
The Canadian Environmental Protection Act is the prime instrument of environmental protection in Canada and the cornerstone of the Government's efforts to protect the environment. These efforts are assisted by other effective legislation including the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, which sets standards for the packaging and labelling of toxic substances and waste for transportation in Canada. The Motor Vehicle Safety Act, another federal Act, also enables the Government to restrict exhaust gas emissions of cars, trucks and buses, to avoid the problems caused by smog and ground level ozone. As we announced on April 21, our Government will reinforce its current international standards on exhaust gas emissions.
The Pest Control Products Act is also part of the environmental arsenal. Its purpose is to screen pesticides and herbicides before their use in Canada. To ensure that environmental concerns are given due consideration, we have started a review of the Pest Control Products Act.
As further proof of our comitment to environmental protection, we intend to add legislation on environmental and water quality assessment to the instruments I mentioned earlier.
In addition to these legal measures, our Government has initiated round table discussions, attracting representatives from industry, public interest groups and government, to establish connection between environmental concerns and decisions made for purposes of economic development.
As for environmental clean-ups, Mr. Speaker, our Government is also trying to eliminate the pollution caused by past carelessness or failure to act. On April 19, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) inaugurated a new era in the treatment of waste substances and the pollution problems they cause. With the provinces, we will set aside $250 million for cleaning up abandoned dumps. Everything will be done to find those responsible and make them foot the bill for the clean-

May 16, 1989
The Environment
up. This is important work that will be done at many dumps in the provinces and the territories.
In eveiy case, our instructions will be to see to it that the polluter pays the cost of corrective measures. However, if the guilty party cannot be found, the Government is prepared to take corrective action as required and to do so promptly.
Mr. Speaker, we also want to upgrade water quality in the Great Lakes. More than $125 million has been spent on this activity. We are now working on the Niagara River and Hamilton harbour. We have also earmarked $110 million for cleaning up waters downstream in the St. Lawrence river. This initiative will be matched by others on the part of the industry and by additional funding.
In 1988 we started to clean up the tar ponds in Sydney, Nova Scotia. Sysco, the polluter in this case, is taking an active part in the clean-up. Still in Nova Scotia, we are examining the pollution problem in Halifax harbour.
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today is a very interesting one but, as you can see, what it proposes is already there in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, the cornerstone of federal environmental legislation. The best way to use our Government's time and resources would be to take effective steps against polluters, using the instruments provided by the legislation, instead of discussing proposals for measures that are already in our federal legislation.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should provide criminal sanctions against corporate officers who knowingly allow their companies to violate government environmental regulations or otherwise endanger the health and safety of Canadians.
I am pleased to support this motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). I think it focuses on the fact that crimes against our environment are really crimes against the people of Canada. The proposal in this motion which can be implemented in legislation would send a very clear signal to the industry right throughout Canada, a signal for the Government of
Canada to take the issue of environmental pollution very seriously indeed.
We have seen environment come from a word that very few people understood a few years ago until the Silent Spring by Rachael Carson came out which first made us the aware that problems were on the horizon. We had later works by the Club of Rome and the Brundtland commission report. These documents have outlined the very serious global nature of the problem we face as a country. Through the implementation of this kind of legislation, Canada would have a marvellous opportunity to lead the way by demonstrating to other nations throughout the world that it is time to take decisive action against those entities that continue to defile our environment to the ultimate expense of mankind. It would be a perfect opportunity for Canada to become a leader in environmental legislation.
The motion before us provides a legislative mechanism to force major polluters to recognize the very serious nature of the problem. I know my time is very limited, but I want to point out that 50 per cent of marine pollution in Canada comes from one industrial source, the pulp mills, and much of that pollution is extremely toxic. Chlorinated hydrocarbons, dioxins, organophos-phates and very poisonous, dangerous compounds, once in the food chain, accumulate in organisms higher up the food chain, ultimately becoming lethal. It is through that bio-concentration that the problems of pollution begin to manifest themselves. We have relied for far too long on the fallacious argument that dilution is the solution, because it no longer holds true.
There are many miles of coastline in Canada, both on the west and the east coasts. It is the intertidal zones that generate the majority of the carbon fixation that takes place on this planet, the photosynthesis, the production of oxygen as it comes out of the oceans and into the air. The first 100 feet of ocean water is the area where most of the pollution impacts upon. In fact, we are endangering intertidal life with continual pollution of pulp mills and many other industrial sources. This is something we continue to ignore, simply because we cannot see it happening and if we cannot see it, it cannot be there. That is no longer true.
May 16, 1989

If we destroy our marine life, and we are in the process of doing so, we will knock out a very crucial link in the web of life. It is time that we came down hard on those industries that continue to ignore this very serious reality that faces us. I am talking not only about industries but about cities and municipalities that continue to dump raw sewage into inland waters, lakes and oceans. Vancouver, for example, dumps 200 million gallons of raw sewage a day. That has an incredible impact on the west coast environment. Other cities throughout Canada also dump untreated raw sewage into inland waters and oceans. That has to stop. Towns and municipalities across Canada are guilty, as well as major corporations, of taking part in this ongoing process of pollution and concentrations of toxins in the environment.
These companies and municipalities will not change their ways unless we get serious and put some teeth into environmental legislation. One way of putting teeth into the legislation is by adopting this motion that my colleague has put before the House today. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me the opportunity to address this motion.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS - MOTIONS   THE ENVIRONMENT PROPOSED CRIMINAL SANCTIONS-VIOLATION OF REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as always, it is an honour and a privilege to speak to the House of Commons on such an important issue.
The Hon. Member's motion reflects the current intolerance of the Canadian people for corporate behaviour which causes damage to the environment or endangers human life or health. Society's revulsion for such conduct is expressed in various federal statutes and particularly in the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, otherwise known as CEPA. Jail terms and fines are among the array of sanctions provided for in CEPA, sanctions commonly understood as being criminal, as the Hon. Member would agree. A contravention of any provision of the Act will expose the offender to the possibility of, at the very least, a fine of $200,000 plus six months in prison.
One offence is actually prosecuted under the Criminal Code and the penalty is up to life in prison and an unlimited fine. This sanction is possible on conviction for a contravention of CEPA where the offender has shown wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of other persons and, thereby, has caused death or bodily harm to another person.
The Environment
For some offences, there is a $1 million fine plus five years in prison. Section 115 of CEPA closely parallels the recommendation in the Law Reform Commission study paper on crimes against the environment wherein two new Criminal Code offences were proposed. Section 115(1) of CEPA creates offences of intentionally or recklessly causing a disaster that results in the loss of use of the environment and showing wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of others, thereby causing a risk of death or harm to another person. These offences are indictable and give rise to liability to an unlimited fine plus five years in prison. For the more serious offence in contravention of CEPA where the offender has shown wanton or reckless disregard for the lives or safety of other persons and thereby causes death or bodily harm to another person, the Act provides for prosecution and conviction under the Criminal Code where the liability is life in prison plus an unlimited fine.
Offences that continue for more than one day give rise to liability to prosecution for a separate offence for each day with the accompanying multiple exposure to fines and imprisonment for each conviction. Special provision is made for officers, directors and agents of a corporation who in any way participated in or were made aware of but did nothing to prevent the commission of an offence by the corporation. Such corporate officials are parties to and guilty of the offence and are liable to the punishment for the offence, whether or not the corporation is prosecuted or convicted.
The Act also simplifies the proof of such offences by corporations by providing that it is sufficient to establish that the offence was committed by an employee or agent of the accused corporation, whether or not the employee or agent is identified or prosecuted for the offence.
CEPA takes into account the position of the Law Reform Commission on the criminalization of certain environmental offences and, in fact in some circumstances, provides for prosecution and conviction under the Criminal Code.
The federal Government has not made a final decision in respect to environmental crimes, although options under consideration include amendments to the Criminal Code, amendments to federal regulatory legislation such as the Fisheries Act, Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, Oil and Gas Conservation Act, Pest Control Products Act, and omnibus legislation amending all federal laws that are directed to the protection of human health and the environment. Because this matter is under very active review and consideration by the federal

May 16, 1989
Adjournment Debate
Government, I find that the Hon. Member's motion is redundant and cannot therefore recommend its adoption by this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
subtopic: FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-INTERPRETATION OF UNFAIR SUBSIDIES-PARTICIPATION OF PROVINCES IN NEGOTIATIONS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 18, in reaction to statements by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) regarding provincial participation in subsidy negotiations with the U.S. Government, I asked the Minister two things.
What is the Canadian definition of subsidy, given that the U.S. definition is well known and being directed in countervail cases against provincial programs? Why then not include the provinces in these subsidy negotiations.
There are three reasons for asking these questions.
First, contrary to the Minister's statement that these negotiations are purely a federal matter, provinces do have a well established constitutional role when it comes to international treaties. Second, federal-provincial consultation during the negotiations that led to the FTA was clearly inadequate. Third, the federal Government's performance to date ought to make us very suspicious of its capacity and determination to defend Canadian interests on its own.
On April 18, the Minister for Trade told this House that he did not intend to let the provinces participate in subsidy negotiations. He said:
We believe quite clearly that international trade is under federal
jurisdiction.
If this is the Minister's position, he is forgetting some rather fundamental Canadian constitutional law.

I remind the Minister of the following fact: the implementation of an international agreement signed by the federal Government requires the willing participation of the provinces. The situation in the United States is obviously quite different. For our southern neighbours, President Bush must have any international agreement ratified by the American Senate. As a result, this treaty automatically amends the relevant American laws, by virtue of article 6 of their Constitution.
In other words, the U.S. federal government has the power to bind the individual states. In Canada, the situation is quite different. An agreement that requires changing the laws of the land can only be implemented by promulgating laws to make those changes. This is not an automatic process.
Does the federal Parliament have the authority to promulgate such laws if they infringe on provincial powers? Certainly not. That has been clear since the 1937 Privy Council Labour Conventions decision. In it, the Privy Council ruled that if a law needed to implement a treaty falls under one of the subjects listed in Section 92 of our Constitution, only a province can pass such a law. This has important consequences for the subsidy negotiations, for if it were decided that some provincial subsidies were unfair, the federal Government could not legislate to abolish them. Neither could the federal Government force the provinces to do so. The provinces would have to agree, but they would certainly have the option not to comply with the demands of the federal Government.

The provinces therefore had a definite constitutional claim to be included in the negotiations. Furthermore, if the federal Government is serious about protecting Canadian interests, the provinces could prove to be
May 16, 1989

useful watch dogs. It is obvious this help would be needed, given the Government's previous track record.
Consultation with the provinces during two years of FTA negotiation was far from adequate. A blatant example of this is that 24 hours to 48 hours prior to the signing of the Accord, provincial trade reps had been told that energy provisions would not be included. They were told that this would be far too complicated. Imagine their surprise when they finally held the Accord in then-hands and discovered a chapter on energy had been included.
The Minister for Trade has recently said that subsidy negotiations would proceed in the same manner as with the FTA. It should be clear from the example I have given that this is not good enough.
Moreover, if we look more closely at the Accord's energy subsidy provisions, we find yet another reason to let the provinces participate in the negotiations. Allowing for subsidies in energy was clearly to the advantage of the United States. In most areas of Canada-United States energy trade, energy flows from north to south. This means that we are allowed to subsidize the exploitation of our energy resources with Canadian taxpayers' money.
However, Article 904(b) of the Free Trade Agreement forbids us to charge Americans more for that energy than we charge ourselves. In other words, Canadians pay for their energy twice. Tax money pays for the exploitation of the resources, then Canadians pay again to buy that energy. Americans only pay once.
If the Government is serious about defending Canadian social and regional development programs in future subsidy negotiations with the United States, the provinces could have a useful role. They could assist Canadian negotiators by acting as a backstop. The negotiators would simply be prevented from unwittingly sacrificing Canadian interests by objections from the provinces. This would help to reassure Canadians that our interests are indeed being defended.

speechtext:

to the concerns of the Member on the Free Trade Agreement. As Hon. Members are aware, Canada and the United States were unable to reach an agreement on changes to our respective subsidy and trade remedy practices during negotiations leading to the conclusion of the Free Trade Agreement. As the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) has pointed out, while these are indeed important issues for discussion we do not intend to be rushed. No negotiations have begun. No demands have been made by either side.
Within the operations branch of the Department of External Affairs a unit has been established to support the Canadian side of the working group. The Minister has indicated that the Canadian chairperson for the working group will be named shortly.
The issue of appropriate international disciplines for subsidy and countervailing measures is a complex one. The subsidies countervail code agreed to during the Tokyo Round of multilateral trade negotiations provided only limited progress toward the goal of international discipline. The issue is under intense scrutiny again in Geneva as part of the current Uruguay NTN Round. Much of the preparatory work being done in this regard will serve us well in the bilateral context, as well as our experience with these negotiations as they progress.
With respect to definition, authorities both in Canada and in the United States responsible for the administration of our respective countervailing duty laws have made determinations of what constitutes a subsidy in specific cases. Under the GATT we have the right to challenge the consistency of American laws with their intemational commitments.
Finally, determinations of subsidy can now be reviewed under the FTA by a binational panel, which we are confident will ensure greater fairness in the application of existing trade remedy laws.
I would suggest that it is premature to attempt to anticipate the position that either we or the United States will be taking in eventual negotiations, or whether

As the Minister for International Trade has pointed out, from the FTA negotiations there appears to be a wide gap between our views and that of the Americans on some of these matters. That does not lead one to expect that a solution will be found very quickly.

In carrying out this responsibility the Government-

subtopic: THE BUDGET-IMPACT OF CLOSURE OF CF BASE AT SUMMERSIDE, RE.I.
THE BUDGET-IMPACT OF CLOSURE OF CF BASE AT SUMMERSIDE, RE.I.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Prince Edward Islanders and all Canadians realized before the "Great Budget Leak" that they would be asked to make a sacrifice to help reduce the national debt. They were prepared to pay their share. They knew the time was coming to pay the piper, and they were willing to join with Canadians to make do with less in order to assist the Government of Canada to get out of the financial mess it refused to address over the past four years.
However, they were not and are not prepared to pay five times the price being asked of other Canadians. They were not and are not prepared to sustain a critical blow to the economy of the province and a mortal blow to the economy of western Prince Edward Island.
Prince Edward Islanders were not, have never been, and are not prepared to accept the closure of Canadian Forces Base Summerside. In the words of a past Deputy
Minister of Finance: "CFB Summerside means as much to Prince Edward Island as the automotive industry does to Ontario".
Therefore, I conclude that the Government did not know what it was actually doing when it made the decision to close CFB Summerside.
Canadian Forces Base Summerside, which is located in the Village of St. Eleanors, and the RCAF base in Mount Pleasant were established during the Second World War to train flyers for overseas duty.
These bases were established by the Minister of War, Colonel James Ralston, the Member of Parliament from Prince which is now Egmont, and a native of Nova Scotia. These bases played a crucial role in advanced training for our fighter pilots which were desperately needed in Europe during World War II.
After that War, the Mount Pleasant facility was abandoned, leaving St. Eleanors as the only military facility in Prince Edward Island.
In 1980 the Minister of National Defence, the Hon. Gilles Lamontagne, made a government commitment that every province would have at least one regular forces base.
What happened to that commitment? The Government has abandoned that commitment under the guise of fiscal restraint.
What happened to the statement by the Hon. Member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) that "there is no question that defence is an important economic tool" and "there is no question regional development will be taken into account"? What happened to the statement in the White Paper on defence which stated at page 85:
Defence programs also make a significant contribution to overcoming regional economic disparities. Over the years, it has been frequently possible to use scarce defence dollars to strengthen local and regional economies while at the same time satisfying defence requirements.
The following statement is also found in the Government's While Paper on defence. At page 84 it states:
Defence expenditures in Canada contribute economic benefits to all sectors of Canadian society.
In fiscal year 1985-86 defence spending accounted for approximately $12 billion of Gross Domestic Product. It produced $1.6 billion in taxes and generated approximately 294,000 jobs, 178,000 in the private sector. Is
May 16, 1989

Prince Edward Island not entitled to any of this spending and any of this job creation?
Let me briefly state what the economic impact will be to Summerside and Prince Edward Island: 1,304 direct jobs will be lost; 1,730 private sector jobs will be lost, for a total of 3,034 jobs, which is 5.39 per cent of the total number of jobs in the province.
Furthermore, base employment supports 5,500 people or 34 per cent of the entire Summerside area population. An annual payroll and expenditure of more than $50 million will be lost. Closure of the base will remove a minimum of 33 per cent of the total income from the Summerside area. In other words, $1 in every $3 would disappear.
St. Eleanors will lose 40 per cent of its tax revenues. The province will lose over $20 million in tax revenue out of a total budget of $167 million, which is one-eighth of its total budget. This is the economic impact. The social impact would be equally devastating.
Many questions are yet to be answered. Who will do fisheries surveillance? Where will search and rescue go? Will the medic-vac service be lost to P.E.I? Does P.E.I have a constitutional right to have a regular forces base? What will happen to our environmental response on the East Coast? What will happen to the monitoring of drug smuggling on the East Coast?
Obviously the province cannot sustain the loss of our Canadian Forces Base. I am sure you will agree that the price we are being asked to pay is too great.
It is often not appreciated or understood that Prince Edward Island is a very small province where even minor readjustment in government policy has a major effect on the province.
For example, take the changes to the unemployment insurance system. Our major industries are all seasonal. Farming, fishing and tourism, in which the majority of our people are engaged, are seasonal activities. It is impossible to fish lobster in the months of December, January, February, March, and April because the gulf is full of ice. Therefore, all people who are engaged in fishing are without work for the winter months. They depend on unemployment insurance.
Adjournment Debate
Yet with the changes in the present system, Prince Edward Island will have a 10.3 per cent negative impact. The nation's net negative impact is 5.6 per cent. P.E.I. will have double the nation's negative impact and more than double the Atlantic impact of 4.7 per cent.
The closure of CFB Summerside cannot be allowed to happen.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: THE BUDGET-IMPACT OF CLOSURE OF CF BASE AT SUMMERSIDE, RE.I.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today all Canadians are being asked to make sacrifices because of our large and growing debt. The Department of National Defence has not been excluded and, in fact, has been asked to slow its spending.
I would like to remind the Hon. Member that the first goal of defence spending is the protection of national security and sovereignty. To achieve that goal during this period of restraint some very difficult decisions had to be taken. Seven bases and stations will be closed along with the reduction in size of seven others. No one likes to close military bases. I can assure the Hon. Member that the decision to close CFB Summerside was not taken lightly.
Most of Canada's fleet of Tracker aircraft operate out of CFB Summerside along with a search and rescue squadron. The Trackers are now over 30 years old. Maintenance has become extremely costly and difficult.
By 1992, only three years away, these aircraft will need to be re-engined to keep them flying. As well, the fuel they require will no longer be readily available. In other words, the aircraft will be obsolete.
For these reasons, along with fiscal restraints, the decision was made to retire the Trackers, which meant that there was no further purpose for CFB Summerside but to close it.
Civilian employees who are presently working at CFB Summerside will be assisted to find alternate employment through our Workforce Adjustment Program. I can assure the Hon. Member that it is a generous package that will be provided to the employees.
Yesterday in this Chamber the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mrs. Collins) pointed out that the military base is not the only option for Prince Edward
