Islanders. She called upon Members to participate in the task force to work with the community to look at alternative development for Prince Edward Island.
I am confident that through the combined efforts of this task force an alternative can be found to the base, one that will provide economic stability to the people of the area of Summerside.

subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-FUNDING OF REAL WOMEN ORGANIZATION
STATUS OF WOMEN-FUNDING OF REAL WOMEN ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 17 last, Equality Day, I raised a very important and crucial issue, one that faces all women in Canada. I am speaking, of course, about the issue of employment equity or, perhaps in these unhappy circumstances, employment inequity.
I was concerned at the time about the glib response provided by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) to the question I raised. At that time she could only say that it was her Party and not mine that had tabled employment equity legislation, making the current provisions passed in Bill C-62 sound as if they had completely solved this terrible problem. Nothing could be further from the truth. Not only is this legislation riddled with flaws, but it also fails utterly to provide the fundamental enforcement mechanism that can effectively protect Canadian women.
I would like to take a few minutes to examine the Minister's assertion that the Government has introduced legislation that is responding to the need for equity in the workplace. Employment equity is the foundation of gender equity. Unfortunately, in spite of some progress made by women, particularly in areas of non-traditional employment, equal pay for work of equal value remains a far-off dream for the majority of working females in Canada.
To make matters worse, groups such as REAL Women continue to fight against equality, charging that women are not equal to men in certain areas. Surely this is the greatest betrayal of women's interests, and the funding of this group is an admission by Government of its lack of belief in equality for women.
Reading REAL'S testimony in which they present their incredibly dinosaur-like views, I am truly astounded that
the Secretary of State could consider funding such a group whose views fly in the face of everything for which women continue to fight. I can assure you that employment equity is not the sole area in which REAL are out of step with the mainstream of Canadian women. They fall behind on child care, on women's participation in active combat duty, in the workforce, and the list goes on.
Employment equity received thoughtful and meaningful treatment when it was dealt with in a variety of committees including the parliamentary committee on equality rights, a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. In their comprehensive and far-reaching report, this committee fleshed out very effectively the evolution of the employment equity debate as it has evolved in Canada.
Employment equity has a solid foundation in Canada's constitutional law, which continues to point Canadian legislators in the direction of comprehensive and far-reaching legal regimes that enshrine equality in the workplace. The Charter pays specific attention to a number of designated groups such as disabled persons, native people, visible minorities and, of course, women.
All groups that have studied the issue and who have testified before the various committees studying employment equity are agreed as to how extensive inequality in the workplace actually is.
The picture, however, while not altogether bleak, needs the active attention of the Minister and of her Government.
Section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms specifically says that special programs for assuring employment equity do not constitute a discriminatory practices. Under Section 15, the Human Rights Commission can be called upon to assist employers who want to adopt special programs for employment equity.
The Human Rights Commission has published some useful guidelines called "Special Programs in Employment: Criteria for Compliance", but few employers have used these guidelines to set up meaningful programs. What is needed is enforcement and contract compliance, elements which are sorely lacking in this Government's employment equity legislation.
May 16, 1989

The issue is a simple one. How can women be protected from discrimination in the workplace when there are no provisions for such enforcement?
Many of the witnesses testifying before parliamentaiy committees on equality rights were sharply critical of the shortcomings of Bill C-62 for these reasons. One, Ms. Shari Stein from the Coalition for Employment Equity stated: "One of our main areas of concern is the lack of an enforcement mechanism in the proposals-what essentially was announced is a voluntary equity program. This means that employees should be encouraged-not required by law rather encouraged-to implement employment equity programs. The only mandatory feature of the proposal is a mandatory reporting requirement for certain kinds of employers. Without an enforcement agency the proposal is just not going to work and I would hate to be back here five years from now sitting in this same chair and saying that the proposal just hasn't worked."
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, we now find ourselves nearly five years down the road, and I am sure that Ms. Stein, if she were given a chance to testify again today, would be equally disappointed as she was when she testified before the parliamentary committee.
I reiterate my call to the Minister of Employment and Immigration to take these concerns seriously and to introduce compliance and enforcement measures that give teeth to the legislation and that give Canadian women meaningful equality in the workplace.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: STATUS OF WOMEN-FUNDING OF REAL WOMEN ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in her question the Hon. Member for Halifax (Ms. Clancy) stated that in 1984 the Government promised Canadian women both employment equity legislation and contract compliance in those areas of the private sector under federal Government influence. That is very important. Then the Hon. Member asked: "Why must we wait and when will this waiting end", and the Minister pointed out that of course the waiting has ended.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the federal contractors program applies to those companies doing business with the federal Government who are not covered by the Employment Equity Act. That is to say, those contractors who are not subject to federal regulations. The program was initiated in 1986 and requires that federal Government suppliers of goods and services with more than 100 employers bidding on Government contracts worth $200,000 or more commit themselves to implement employment equity as a condition of their bid. Suppliers
Adjournment Debate
who make an employment equity commitment and who are awarded contracts will be subject to on site reviews. Since 1986, more than 175 compliance reviews have been initiated and 30 are now completed.
The Minister of State for Employment and Immigration (Mrs. Vezina) has advised me that altogether somewhere around 1,173 employers, representing 897,359 employees, have signed certificates of commitment to implement employment equity under the Federal Contractors Program. Of these, 582 contractors representing a total labour force of 693,283 employees are subject to review by virtue of having won government contracts. More and more companies are coming into the program every day as new contracts are awarded. Companies may be denied the opportunity to bid on future government contracts until such time as they have implemented an employment equity plan.
All companies falling under the Federal Contractors Program are required to develop comprehensive employment equity plans by which to improve the representation in the work force of women, aboriginal people, visible minorities and persons with disabilities.
The process of employment equity is well under way. Already we see positive developments in attitudes toward hiring and promoting members of the designated groups. The nearly 150 compliance reviews now under way and the 30 already concluded confirm this. However, changing the proportionate numbers in a company's work force cannot be achieved overnight.
The Employment Equity Act is landmark legislation. For the first time we have a benchmark and we have benchmark data against which Canadians can judge a company's progress in the area of equity. With the Federal Contractors Program we can determine where discrimination exists. We can initiate investigations under the Canadian Human Rights Act and these investigations are not based on allegations but on basic precise data. Action was taken in the area of equity, progress is being made and our work force will be more representative of the people of Canada in the future.
